saussure.label: Structural linguistics
saussure.date_label: Saussure’s Course, posthumous, 1916 · later linguistic programmes
saussure.description: Relational signs, language states and historical change, phonological analysis, and social uses of language form distinct inquiries. Later semiology, anthropology, psychoanalysis and historical debates adapt and criticize particular concepts.
saussure.representative_figures_and_works: Saussure’s Course in General Linguistics (1916, posthumous); Roman Jakobson is an important intermediary for Lévi-Strauss.

representative_people.context: Relational value, social convention and distinct analyses of language states and change. The posthumous Course is an editorial reconstruction of teaching, not a finished authorial manuscript.

representative_people.context: A named resource in Lévi-Strauss’s phonological analogy; the chapter warns against literal transfer to kinship. His analysis of selection and combination also differentiates metaphoric and metonymic operations.
representative_people.works: “Principien der historischen Phonologie” (1931); “Observations sur le classement phonologique des consonnes” (1938); Kindersprache, Aphasie und allgemeine Lautgesetze (1941), cited in Structural Anthropology; “Two Aspects of Language and Two Types of Aphasic Disturbances” (selected reprint, pp. 95–114)

representative_people.context: Reworks langue/parole through schema, norm and usage; Barthes explicitly discusses this reformulation. His formal programme is distinct from Meillet’s social explanation.

saussure.scope_note: A selective teaching umbrella, not one uniform school or a claim that all linguistics descends from Saussure. The Course is posthumously reconstructed; Meillet’s social explanation, phonological programmes and Hjelmslev’s formal distinctions differ. Later reception is separately evidenced. Benveniste and broader linguistic traditions remain review gaps.

epistemology.label: Historical epistemology
epistemology.description: Here the label denotes the French tradition associated with Bachelard and Canguilhem: histories of scientific concepts, norms, and discontinuities. It informs Foucault through a route distinct from structural linguistics. It is not an umbrella for every historical or sociological account of scientific knowledge. Bachelard’s own preliminary discourse distinguishes normative epistemology from a chronological history and calls its period labels approximate. Canguilhem’s norm/average discussion draws on Halbwachs and human geography; his later preface distinguishes newly encountered works from resources actually used in1943.
epistemology.representative_figures_and_works: French history and philosophy of science; this connection prevents treating Foucault as merely a descendant of structural linguistics. Bachelard, La formation de l’esprit scientifique (1938); Canguilhem, the normal/pathological essay (1943; expanded 1966) and La formation du concept de réflexe (1955).

economic.label: Economic history
economic.date_label: 1800s roots · Economic History Society founded 1926 · multiple paradigms
economic.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
economic.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000). E. A. Wrigley: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988).

strands.title: Market norms and popular action
strands.focus: Thompson asks how customary expectations authorize or constrain protest and exchange; Mintz supplies a named anthropological resource. This is a situated inquiry into English crowds, not a universal premarket economy.
strands.works: “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

strands.title: Agrarian change and documentary comparability
strands.focus: Tawney distinguishes regional and temporal patterns, tenant and landlord activity, legal forms and economic pressures. His introduction treats incomplete statistics and incompatible records as problems of inference.
strands.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

strands.title: Women’s work, household forms and economic change
strands.focus: Clark and Pinchbeck distinguish home production from wages, while differing over the timing and consequences of economic change. Their acknowledgments make research guidance and shared materials part of this scholarship.
strands.works: Working Life of Women (1919); Women Workers (1930)

strands.title: Domestic service as an economic question
strands.focus: Salmon connects household employment with industrial specialization and challenges its reduction to a private complaint. Her historical model and proposed remedies are arguments to assess, not a universal account of women’s experience.
strands.works: Domestic Service (1897), chapters I–II; Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

strands.title: Brazilian income flows and structural criticism
strands.focus: Furtado’s coffee-crisis argument connects demand and historical change; Novais asks how wage labour and capitalism’s formation explain the transformation. Their exchange keeps macroeconomic analysis open to historical criticism.

strands.title: Managerial coordination and the scale of activity
strands.focus: Chandler’s selected opening links new energy, transport and communication capacities to the conditions for administrative coordination. Earlier growth and specialization could remain compatible with owner-managed firms and market exchange.
strands.works: The Visible Hand (1977), Part I and chapter1 opening

strands.title: Artisans and uneven industrialization in India
strands.focus: Roy examines five crafts rather than treating textile decline as universal. His introduction distinguishes family work, wage labour, markets and organizational change, while acknowledging that adaptation did not yield development comparable to Europe or Japan.
strands.works: Traditional Industry in the Economy of Colonial India (1999), introduction

strands.title: Firms, inventions and forms of work
strands.focus: Compare Chandler’s American enterprise scale, Mokyr’s British technological change and Roy’s Indian artisanal reorganization. These explanations concern different units and periods; none supplies a universal sequence from household to large factory.
strands.works: Chandler (1977); Mokyr (1999); Roy (1999), selected primary passages

strands.title: Railroads and the meaning of social saving
strands.focus: McClelland contests identifying measured transport savings with the railroad’s entire contribution to growth. His notes question the relation between observed freight prices and marginal costs under altered traffic and competition.
strands.works: Railroads and American Economic Growth (1964); McClelland (1968), opening and notes

strands.title: Slavery productivity and a contested inference
strands.focus: Fogel and Engerman’s opening specifies a total-factor-productivity index. David and Temin argue that national-price aggregation across differing crop mixes need not rank technical efficiency: climate, prices and risk complicate the inference.

strands.title: Household production and disputed divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz challenges Huang’s involution thesis and compares household labor with industrious change. Huang’s 2002 review argues that output growth can conceal diminishing returns to work; Pomeranz’s reply opening rejects one necessary path to development.
strands.works: Pomeranz (2000),17; Huang and Pomeranz (2002), selected retrospective passages; Huang’s rejoinder and Pomeranz’s response (2003)

strands.title: Coal, constraints and competing explanations
strands.focus: Pomeranz links accessible energy and colonial resources to relief of land constraints. Huang questions whether coal availability explains divergence or industrial demand explains coal development. The exchange leaves causal weights open to examination.

strands.title: Wealth and the measurement of goods
strands.focus: Weatherill acknowledges Shammas’s challenge: ownership patterns associated with occupation or towns may reflect wealth. Their different data constructions ask different questions.

strands.title: Agrarian labour and recorded categories
strands.focus: Kumar’s southern Indian inquiry combines documentary interpretation with quantitative reconstruction. Her stated caste/occupation assumptions must remain visible when discussing estimates.
strands.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts I,IV,X

strands.title: Population and the character of industrial growth
strands.focus: Wrigley investigates population change and the contingent character of industrial growth. This bounded summary follows the Economic History Society account and the publisher excerpts of Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, pp. 1–8) and Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010, pp. 1–6, 9–11); People, Cities and Wealth (1987) is unread.
strands.works: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988)

economic.scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Institutional approaches are not interchangeable, and consumption does not replace production. Household interests can conflict. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.

military.label: Military history
military.date_label: Earlier roots · Howard 1961 · Keegan 1976 · multiple paradigms
military.description: Studies campaigns and combat alongside institutions, societies, maritime power, gender and remembrance. Ancient historians such as Thucydides and Polybius already wrote about testing reports of battle, terrain and military experience; they are precursors of the genre, not its founders. From about 1900 the field was practised in archive-based campaign and army histories, university lectureships and chairs (Oxford 1905 and 1909), official histories of the world wars and an American society (1933) and journal (1937; renamed Military Affairs in 1941); much of this work was written by or for officers. Howard’s contextual reconstruction, Keegan’s critical study of battle and debates over military revolutions supply different methods and explanations. Source access, narrative framing and geographic scope shape their claims.
military.representative_figures_and_works: Ancient precursors include Thucydides and Polybius on testing reports, terrain and experience; modern roots include Clausewitz, On War (1832), and Hans Delbrück; from c. 1900, Charles Oman and J. W. Fortescue wrote archive-based campaign and army history, Grundy and Kromayer surveyed ancient battlefields, and general-staff and cabinet historical sections wrote official histories of the world wars (Edmonds from 1922; the US Army’s World War II series, such as Matloff and Snell, 1953); later examples: Michael Howard, John Keegan, and Joanna Bourke.

representative_people.context: Examines political purpose, passion, chance and friction in an unfinished, posthumously edited work. Strategic reasoning differs from empirical verification of particular campaigns.
representative_people.works: On War (1832); selected passages in Graham translation with later editorial apparatus

representative_people.context: Joins philological criticism to checks of practical possibility, using population evidence and documentary research. Explicitly acknowledges Ranke and Beloch; possible reconstructions are not automatically established events.
representative_people.works: Geschichte der Kriegskunst im Rahmen der politischen Geschichte, four volumes (1900–1920); first preface (1900); Numbers in History (London lectures, 1913)

representative_people.context: Combines campaign reconstruction, wider social context and war-studies teaching. Archival loss/access constrained the 1961 study; later Ultra disclosure exposed limits of official Grand Strategy records.
representative_people.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); Grand Strategy, IV (1972); War in European History (1976); with John Sparrow, The Coldstream Guards 1920–1946 (1951); “Military History as a University Study” (1956), as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch; “The Use and Abuse of Military History” (lecture 1961; RUSI Journal 1962), reported by Kitchen and Mitchell (2022), Strachan (2002) and Speller (2012)

representative_people.context: Studies combat experience through critically assessed testimony, documents and physical possibility. Sandhurst teaching, Delbrück/Burne and scholarly/library assistance inform the work; his battle definition leaves much colonial and guerrilla experience outside its frame.
representative_people.works: The Face of Battle (1976), available opening excerpt; A History of Warfare (1993), separate argument mediated by Bassford

representative_people.context: Studies bodily injury, disease and masculinity in Britain during and after the Great War.
representative_people.works: Dismembering the Male (1996)

representative_people.context: Builds the opening-war narrative around decisions and circumstances. Her methodological excerpt insists on documented detail; the full Guns of August source apparatus remains to be collated.
representative_people.works: The Guns of August (1962); “In Search of History,” publisher excerpt in Practicing History (consulted 1982 edition)

representative_people.context: Combines campaigns, diplomacy and narrative; her German-centered framing of the Thirty Years War attracts criticism.
representative_people.works: The Thirty Years War (1938); “The Strategy of the Great Civil War” (1945)

representative_people.works: “The ‘Military Revolution,’ 1560–1660—a Myth?” (1976; revised 1979); The Military Revolution (1988); The Thirty Years War (1984), pp. xv, 216–217, mediated by Woolrych

representative_people.works: The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890), preface

representative_people.context: Named colleague and source of a recounted practical drill experiment; a resource for asking what combat descriptions physically imply.

representative_people.context: Sandhurst librarian acknowledged by Keegan; library work joins interlibrary loans and other research assistance in producing the book.

representative_people.context: Tests his narrative against his own and others’ observation and notes conflicting eyewitness accounts (1.22); at Mantinea he says Spartan secrecy and bragging prevent accurate numbers (5.68). Grundy (1911) calls the work ‘in the main a military history’ whose aim was political teaching. A precursor of the genre, not its founder.
representative_people.works: History of the Peloponnesian War, 1.22 and 5.68 (Crawley translation, 1910)

representative_people.context: Divides systematic history into the study of documents, the survey of places and political experience; holds that no one without experience of war can write well about it; and tests Ephorus’ account of Mantinea against the ground (12.25e–28a). Kromayer (1903, 1928) adopts and qualifies this criticism, and he and Delbrück disputed Polybius’ reliability at Sellasia. Book 12 is fragmentary and polemical.
representative_people.works: Histories 12.25e–28a; 3.33, 3.48 and 3.59 (Paton, Loeb)

representative_people.context: Prefers Ptolemy and Aristobulus because they served on Alexander’s campaign, and Ptolemy also because falsehood would have disgraced a king. Kromayer and Veith (1928) call Arrian and Ptolemy expert sources.
representative_people.works: Anabasis of Alexander, preface (Chinnock translation, 1884)

representative_people.context: Joins philology to topographic survey: an expedition to Greek battlefields in spring 1900 with a General Staff officer released by Schlieffen. Defends Polybius against Delbrück at Sellasia (1903), and observes that each era’s military theory shaped its reading of ancient war (1928). His Hellenistic analogies with the modern great state are his own framing.
representative_people.works: Antike Schlachtfelder in Griechenland, vol. I (1903); with Georg Veith, Heerwesen und Kriegführung der Griechen und Römer (1928)

representative_people.context: Co-author of a handbook whose preface treats Greek and Roman warfare together, adds strategy and tactics to the antiquarian study of armies, and excludes the Orient, Carthage, Gauls and Germans. As quoted in its introduction he contrasts Greek and Roman warfare, citing Delbrück on discipline: national-character generalisations of their time. His battlefield volumes are unread.
representative_people.works: With Johannes Kromayer, Heerwesen und Kriegführung der Griechen und Römer (1928)

representative_people.context: Surveyed Thermopylae, Plataea and Pylos himself (1892–99) to test Herodotus and Thucydides, holding that ‘maps without accuracy cannot be used for the historical criticism of highly elaborate narratives’ (1901); his 1911 preface argues that the strategy of the Ten Years’ War is explicable only on economic grounds.
representative_people.works: The Great Persian War (1901), preface; Thucydides and the History of His Age (1911), preface and introduction

representative_people.context: His preface proposes an institutional history of the legions (organisation, recruitment and terms of service), says he has ‘avoided a detailed account of particular campaigns’ and credits Domaszewski and Ritterling; the abbreviation list shows extensive inscription corpora. The body of the book is unread.
representative_people.works: The Roman Legions (1928)

representative_people.context: Planned a history of the art of war ‘from Greek and Roman times’ (1898), walking battlefields to supplement maps; his Peninsular War (1902) used Record Office papers, including passages omitted from printed dispatches, and treated veterans’ memoirs with ‘very cautious handling’. No influence on or from Delbrück is claimed.
representative_people.works: A History of the Art of War: The Middle Ages (1898), preface; A History of the Peninsular War, vol. I (1902), preface

representative_people.context: A civilian who wrote the army’s history for ‘the political not less than the military aspect’ (1899) and read regimental histories ‘not always with profound respect for their accuracy’. As Trinity College’s first lecturer in military history (1913) he defined it as the strife of communities through ‘organised bands of armed men’, holding that ‘below a certain stage of civilisation, there can be no military history’.
representative_people.works: A History of the British Army, vols. I–II (1899), preface; Military History: Lectures Delivered at Trinity College, Cambridge (1914)

representative_people.context: First Chichele Professor of Military History at Oxford (1909). His inaugural lecture calls military history ‘the effort to understand war’, makes policy, not generalship, ‘the architectonic art’, and holds that ‘as the State is, so will its army be’.
representative_people.works: The University and the Study of War (1909)

representative_people.context: Compiled the British official history of the Western Front in the Committee of Imperial Defence’s Historical Section: ‘based on the British official records’, written partly for ‘students at military schools’, and read in typescript or proof by officers who took part. The preface documents participant review; its effects on the history’s independence are not assessed here. Green (2003) and French (1986) remain unread.
representative_people.works: Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1914, vol. I (1922), preface

representative_people.context: Called history ‘based solely on formal documents’ ‘essentially superficial’ (1930) and official ‘camouflaged history’ ‘the dry rot of armies’ (1944), while placing the war’s decisive history in ‘the cabinets and in the military headquarters’. Strachan (2002) calls him ‘in many ways more a journalist than an academic’, for whom military history was ‘a tool’.
representative_people.works: The Real War, 1914–1918 (1930), preface; Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944)

representative_people.context: A Harvard historian who proposed a naval history of the war to Roosevelt in 1942 and was given the records he wished to consult; he or his assistants took part in operations. The Navy declared the work ‘in no sense an official history’; Morison held that historians with military experience ‘will always be more tolerant of failure’.
representative_people.works: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, vol. II, Operations in North African Waters (1947), foreword and introduction

representative_people.context: A former Brooklyn College history instructor who, with Edwin M. Snell, wrote the US Army’s volume on coalition strategic planning; both had served in the war and joined the War Department’s historical project in 1946. The Chief of Military History’s foreword asks readers to see its controversies as differences ‘among comrades in arms’.
representative_people.works: With Edwin M. Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942 (1953)

representative_people.context: Chief Historian of the US Army’s Office of the Chief of Military History, named by Matloff and Snell as ‘the first and most attentive critic’ of their volume. A named editorial role only; his The Historian and the Army (1954) is unread.
representative_people.works: Chief Historian’s review of Matloff and Snell (1953), as acknowledged in their preface

representative_people.context: Headed the civil series of the British official history of the Second World War from 1941; as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch, he concluded that the armed forces were ‘no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war’. An elector who chose Falls over Liddell Hart for the Chichele chair in 1946. Known here through that article only.
representative_people.works: With Margaret Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Country and Calling (1954), pp. 196–97, as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022)

representative_people.context: Appointed to King’s College London’s new chair of military studies in 1927. His inaugural lecture, as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch, made statecraft, economics, industry and civilian morale part of the study of war and called military history ‘but a special branch of the general study’; Howard used it to structure his 1964 professorial lecture.
representative_people.works: “On the Uses of the Study of War” (inaugural lecture, 1927), as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022)

representative_people.context: Co-author with Hancock of British War Economy (1949), in the civil series of the British official history of the Second World War, as Morgan-Owen and Finch report. Known here through that report only; the book is unread and no argument of hers is assessed.
representative_people.works: With W. K. Hancock, British War Economy (1949), as reported by Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022)

representative_people.context: Records work acknowledged by Matloff and Snell: ‘Nearly every page in the volume bears some mark of Mrs. Bailey’s wide knowledge and exact understanding of the records kept by the War Department’. An acknowledgement of records labour; no work of her own is assessed.
representative_people.works: Records assistance acknowledged in Matloff and Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942 (1953), preface

representative_people.works: Statistical work acknowledged in Matloff and Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942 (1953), preface

military.scope_note: A research field with overlapping objects, not one school or a progression that supersedes campaign history. Delbrück, campaign and army historians, official historians and strategic writers supply distinct resources; military historians also reinterpret and criticize them. Keegan’s restricted battle definition leaves much colonial and guerrilla experience outside its frame. European military-revolution debates extend to overseas encounters without representing the whole world’s military historiography. Bourke, Winter and Nell retain distinct questions about bodies, mourning and recognition. Scholarly collaboration, library work, editing and archival limits are part of the field’s production. Ancient writers who narrated and judged wars (Thucydides, Polybius, Arrian) are selected precursors. The selected ancient passages document statements about testimony, terrain and experience. Separately checked modern passages discuss these authors; Kromayer explicitly engages Polybius’ criticism of Ephorus. These examples do not establish continuous transmission. Clausewitz ranked ancient military history the least useful while allowing instructive exceptions. Official and semi-official histories were written from privileged records, read in proof by participants or framed by sponsoring institutions; Liddell Hart criticised them in the period. Karsten (1984), describing the ‘new’ military history, concedes that ‘some scholars explored such questions in the past’. The selection before 1960 concentrates on British, American and German scholarship; other historiographies of war are not surveyed here.

strands.title: Campaign reconstruction and documentary limits
strands.focus: Howard, Tuchman and Wedgwood connect decisions and circumstances through different narrative practices. Source access and explanatory selection remain objects of criticism.
strands.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); The Guns of August (1962); The Thirty Years War (1938)

strands.title: Combat experience and critical testimony
strands.focus: Keegan joins questions about bodies and behavior to criticism of memoirs, rhetoric and physical possibility. His selected battle frame does not represent all forms of war.
strands.works: The Face of Battle (1976), available excerpt

strands.title: War studies, research and teaching
strands.focus: Howard became lecturer in military studies at King’s in 1953; a new War Studies programme was approved in 1955. His King’s work combines historical study with wider social, ethical and political inquiry. Earlier work and institutional support included Laughton’s naval history, Maurice’s chair of military studies (1927; the department closed in 1948), and C. K. Webster and Hancock, whose official-history work had drawn them to war as a field. Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022) call the story of Howard rescuing the subject from an academic wilderness one he ‘consciously cultivated’. Library access, publishing and translation collaboration form part of the research setting.
strands.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); War in European History (1976)

strands.title: Naval history within wider explanation
strands.focus: Sea power and military/naval coordination widen a land-centered account. Mahan and Corbett state different purposes from a simple naval chronicle.

strands.title: Military revolutions: causes and chronology
strands.focus: Roberts, Parker, Rogers, Black and Lynn debate timing, mechanisms and evidence. Their accounts do not form one settled technological explanation.

strands.title: Finance, bargaining and geographic scope
strands.focus: Fiscal bargaining and overseas comparisons complicate a universal route from weapons to centralized power. The selected debate remains weighted toward European questions.

strands.title: Bodies, injury and masculinity
strands.focus: Bourke examines men’s bodies and wartime masculinity. This question differs from strategic success or adding women to a roster.

strands.title: Remembrance, mourning and recognition
strands.focus: Winter examines forms of mourning; Nell recovers Black military service from patriotic exclusion. These different projects broaden whose war is remembered.
strands.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995); The Colored Patriots (1855)

strands.title: Cultural explanations and their critics
strands.focus: Keegan’s later account and Bassford’s opposition distinguish cultural interpretation from the earlier reconstruction of combat. Political purpose and culture need not be mutually exclusive.
strands.works: A History of Warfare (1993), mediated; Bassford (1994)

strands.title: Recruitment as labor and household strategy
strands.focus: Lucassen and Zürcher compare state recruitment options with recruits’ and households’ responses. Pay and freedom vary independently; different systems coexist. Their explicit use of Tilly connects fiscal capacity to recruitment and resistance.

strands.title: Official and semi-official history and its critics
strands.focus: General-staff and cabinet historical sections wrote large histories of the world wars from privileged records. Edmonds’s British volumes (from 1922) were ‘based on the British official records’, written partly for ‘students at military schools’ and read in proof by officers who took part. Morison’s naval history was commissioned with full records access yet declared ‘in no sense an official history’ (1947). In the US Army’s series, Matloff and Snell, formerly instructors in history and English respectively and both wartime servicemen, joined the project in 1946; their volume’s foreword, by the Chief of Military History, asked readers to see its controversies as differences ‘among comrades in arms’ (1953), and its preface credits Helen McShane Bailey’s knowledge of the War Department’s records and Evelyn Cooper’s statistics. Liddell Hart attacked documentary and ‘camouflaged’ history (1930, 1944). During and after the Second World War official commissions drew academic historians to war (Hancock and Gowing from 1941, Webster and Frankland from 1950, Howard from 1959), under closure rules and secrecy. Later studies of the genre are unread here, and the German and French official histories are known only from period mentions.
strands.works: Edmonds, Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1914, vol. I (1922), preface; Liddell Hart, The Real War (1930), preface, and Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944); Morison, Operations in North African Waters (1947), foreword and introduction; Matloff and Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942 (1953), foreword and preface; Hancock and Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Howard, Grand Strategy, vol. IV (1972)

strands.title: Campaign and army history as scholarship, c. 1898–1950
strands.focus: Oman’s art-of-war volume (1898) and Peninsular War (1902) worked from chronicles, Record Office papers and passages omitted from printed dispatches, treated veterans’ memoirs with caution and walked battlefields. Fortescue, a civilian, wrote the army’s history as political as well as military history (1899) and distrusted regimental histories; his 1914 definition held that ‘below a certain stage of civilisation, there can be no military history’, a boundary that bears on the field’s geographic scope. Parker’s preface (1928) proposes an institutional history of the Roman legions’ organisation, recruitment and service; the abbreviation list shows extensive inscription corpora, and the body is unread. Kromayer and Veith’s preface (1928) adds strategy and tactics to the antiquarian study of ancient armies and excludes the Orient, Carthage, Gauls and Germans. Howard (1961, as reported by Kitchen and Mitchell and by Strachan) later named regimental ‘nursery history’ and the historian’s duty to examine its ‘myth’.
strands.works: Oman, A History of the Art of War: The Middle Ages (1898) and A History of the Peninsular War, vol. I (1902), prefaces; Fortescue, A History of the British Army, vols. I–II (1899), preface, and Military History (1914); Parker, The Roman Legions (1928); Kromayer and Veith, Heerwesen und Kriegführung der Griechen und Römer (1928); Howard, ‘The Use and Abuse of Military History’ (1961 lecture; 1962)

strands.title: Chairs, journals and the soldier-scholar before 1960
strands.focus: In the British institutions examined here, university teaching developed alongside officer education. Oxford made military history a special subject after the South African War, created a lectureship in 1905 and a chair in 1909, whose first holder, Spenser Wilkinson, called military history ‘the effort to understand war’; the chair, vacant from 1939, went to Cyril Falls in 1946 rather than Liddell Hart. Trinity College, Cambridge, appointed Fortescue its first lecturer in military history in 1913. At King’s College London Frederick Maurice held a chair of military studies from 1927; the department closed in 1948. In the United States the American Military History Foundation was incorporated in 1933 after discussions among ‘military and civilian archival personnel’; its journal (1937) became Military Affairs in 1941 and nearly collapsed in 1957. Strachan (2002) calls Liddell Hart and Falls ‘in many ways more a journalist than an academic’ and writes that before Howard’s appointment almost nobody who studied the history of war had not experienced it.
strands.works: Wilkinson, The University and the Study of War (1909); Fortescue, Military History (1914), lecture I; Maurice, ‘On the Uses of the Study of War’ (1927), as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch; Society for Military History chronology (1933–69 entries)

strands.title: War, state and society before the ‘new military history’
strands.focus: Wilkinson’s inaugural lecture (1909) held that ‘as the State is, so will its army be’ and that in war ‘the architectonic art is policy or politics, not strategy or generalship’. Maurice (1927, as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch) counted statecraft, economics, raw materials, science, industry and civilian morale as of ‘prime importance’ to the study of war. Hancock, editing the civil official histories, treated the armed forces as ‘no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war’ (as quoted by the same authors). Roberts (1955) proposed tactical change with wider institutional effects. Quincy Wright’s foreword (1942) describes a study of war begun at the University of Chicago in 1926 that involved ‘over fifty studies by research assistants and members of the faculty’; only the foreword is read. Karsten (1984) calls such questions the ‘new’ military history while conceding that ‘some scholars explored such questions in the past’. Hintze, Vagts, Ritter and Ropp are not yet read for this entry.
strands.works: Wilkinson (1909); Maurice, inaugural lecture (1927); Wright, A Study of War (1942), foreword; Hancock and Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Roberts, ‘The Military Revolution, 1560–1660’ (1955 lecture); Karsten (1984), opening

strands.title: Ancient historians on testimony, terrain and experience
strands.focus: Thucydides tests eyewitness accounts against one another and says Spartan secrecy and bragging prevent accurate numbers at Mantinea. Polybius requires the study of documents, the survey of places and political experience, holds that no one without experience of war can write well about it, and judges Ephorus’ land battles by the ground; his polemic is also self-promotion. Arrian prefers Ptolemy and Aristobulus because they served on the campaign. Grundy (1911) calls Thucydides’ narrative ‘in the main a military history’ subordinated to political teaching, and Kromayer (1903) adopts and qualifies Polybius’ criticism of Ephorus. Delbrück (1913, p. 16) asks: ‘Ought we to believe what Caesar informs us of concerning the gigantic armies of the Gauls, whose conquest is his glory, since we have now seen that neither Napoleon nor Frederick in this respect is to be trusted?’; Caesar’s text itself was not read. Herodotus and Xenophon appear only through modern critics: Delbrück (1913) notes that Herodotus wrote ‘forty or fifty years after the events’, Grundy (1901) that in military matters he ‘seems to have possessed little, if any, special knowledge’, and Kromayer (1903, p. 93) finds Xenophon’s account of Mantinea one-sided. These writers are precursors of a genre, not a single origin of the field.
strands.works: Thucydides, History 1.22, 5.68; Polybius, Histories 12.25e–28a, 3.33, 3.48; Arrian, Anabasis, preface; Grundy (1901), preface, and (1911), pp. 7–9; Kromayer (1903), pp. 93–96; Delbrück, Numbers in History (1913), pp. 8–10, 16

continuation.basis: The field is older and broader than these selected works; ancient precursors are not its beginning, and no researched universal interval is proposed.

chronology.interpretation: Use dated works with an explicit selective scope. Thucydides, Polybius and Arrian are context: precursors of the genre, placed only by century, not a lineage or the field’s first years. Oman, Fortescue, Delbrück, Grundy and Kromayer (1898–1903) are a selected cluster of modern scholarly work, not a foundation date; Kromayer’s 1900 expedition is context for his 1903 volume. Official and semi-official histories (Edmonds 1922, Morison 1947, Matloff and Snell 1953) and the American society and journal (1933, 1937) are selected later events, not the beginnings of official or American military history. Howard 1961 and Keegan 1976 are contributions to an older field, not its first and last years. Later memoir dates are evidence dates, not new personal interventions by Howard.
retain: Multiple paradigms, colonial/guerrilla limits of Keegan's frame, and collaboration/editorial labour.
Ancient precursors are not a continuous lineage; the modern selection concentrates on British, American and German scholarship.
unresolved: If phase bars are useful, define their subject and geography; do not construct a universal beginning from the oldest source in this selection.
Composition dates of the ancient works were not checked; they are placed by century only. Caesar, Herodotus and Xenophon are discussed only through modern critics and are not dated here.

political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.
political.representative_figures_and_works: Ranke is one major nineteenth-century root. Later examples: Lewis Namier, Charles Tilly, and Lynn Hunt’s Politics, Culture, and Class (1984). Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: Voters and competing group explanations

strands.title: Rights movements and political inclusion
strands.focus: Sustained organization for women’s rights is part of political history; it is not merely an appendix to histories of officeholders. strands.title: Collective claims and governing work
strands.focus: Tilly connects performances and repertoires with state/economic change; Cooper asks how colonial labor categories govern social relations. Their regional units and explanations differ.

strands.title: Political rhetoric, symbols and social identities

strands.focus: Davis questions inherited Ranter accounts; Thompson defends a historical milieu; Scott stresses anachronism and Smith disputes both sides’ handling of evidence and theology. These are different positions, not an adjudicated consensus.

biography.scope_note: A genre and set of methods with ancient and varied roots, not inherently great-man history, psychohistory or microstoria. The selected roster combines earlier practices, modern historical work and critics. Davis’s comparison preserves religious and colonial differences; her imagined prologue is not historical testimony. Bourdieu questions narrated coherence without banning life histories; Levi emphasizes choices within constraints and investigates group formation. Biography can explain wider relations, but its scale and source gaps remain subjects of criticism. Non-European traditions and original translation witnesses require further research; the current selection is not exhaustive.

science.label: History of science
science.date_label: Earlier roots · History of Science Society founded 1924 · later approaches
science.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.
science.representative_figures_and_works: George Sarton; Alexandre Koyré, Études galiléennes (1939); Robert K. Merton; Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962); Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985). Yates and Foucault provide additional, distinct contributions; they do not substitute for these historians and programmes. Further approaches include Metzger’s history of chemistry (1923), Maier’s medieval natural philosophy (1949), Fleck’s scientific fact (1935), Needham’s collaborative Chinese science project (from 1954), Rossiter’s Women Scientists in America (1982), and Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980).

Publication credits do not replace primary argument checks; wider regional coverage remains selective. Arabic mathematics, colonial Indian science, African healing and a Beninese knowledge programme are separate selected projects, not regional proxies or exhaustive coverage.

white.label: Hayden White / narrative theory
white.date_label: “The Burden of History” 1966 · Metahistory 1973 · The Content of the Form 1987 · Holocaust emplotment 1992 · reply to Chartier 1995 · “The Practical Past” 2010 · The Practical Past 2014
white.description: Examines how emplotment, argument and tropes organize historical accounts: narrative form helps constitute an interpretation rather than merely decorating established facts. As Herman Paul reads Metahistory (1973), it treats emplotment as one of the ways historians explain, not as a replacement for explanation. His work raises disputes about historical explanation and representation; it should not be reduced to the claim that evidence is irrelevant. He asked what limits govern responsible narratives of the Holocaust (1992, known here through quoted passages), answered Roger Chartier’s four questions about language, tropes, research and relativism (1995), and from 2010 argued, after Michael Oakeshott, for a “practical past” of memories, attitudes and values that people summon “to justify, dignify, excuse, alibi or make a case for actions” (Historein, 2010). Philosophers of history built on and contested his work: Paul (2019) calls it the field’s shared reference point, while Timmins (2011) doubts its impact on historians’ practice, and Ginzburg kept him as a target, as Perry Anderson reads Threads and Traces (2012).
white.representative_figures_and_works: “The Burden of History” (1966); Metahistory: The Historical Imagination in Nineteenth-Century Europe (1973); Tropics of Discourse (1978); “The Value of Narrativity in the Representation of Reality” (1980); The Content of the Form (1987); “Historical Emplotment and the Problem of Truth” (1992); reply to Chartier (1995); Figural Realism (1999); afterword to Beyond the Cultural Turn (1999); “The Historical Event” (2008); “The Practical Past” (2010); The Fiction of Narrative, ed. Robert Doran (2010); The Practical Past (2014). White’s analysis of historical narrative is a distinct contribution within debates grouped here as the linguistic turn. Readings: Paul (2011, through Timmins; 2019); Anderson on Ginzburg (2012); Spiegel (2013, 2018).
white.scope_note: Metahistory’s formalist reading of selected nineteenth-century European works is one project, read here only in its introduction (pp. 1–11); the 1999 afterword also affirms a Marxian commitment. Narrative construction does not erase the distinction between historical and invented events. The 1992 Holocaust essay is represented by passages quoted by Claus and Marriott, an excerpt witness, not by its full argument. “The Practical Past” (2010) and the 1995 rejoinder to Chartier (in authorised Portuguese translation) are read in full. The 2014 book, The Fiction of Narrative, Figural Realism and Paul’s 2011 study are known through contents pages and named readers (Spiegel, Neves, Sanz Loroño, Timmins); the 2005 exchange with Dirk Moses is dated from metadata, and Moses’s argument is unread. The criticisms by Ricoeur, David Carr, Lorenz, Ankersmit and Runia are reported by Paul (2019).

kuhn.label: Thomas Kuhn
kuhn.description: Explains scientific development through normal science, disciplinary commitments, crises, and revolutions. Paradigms organize problems and standards of inquiry. Later sociologists adapt these arguments, sometimes in ways Kuhn disputes; this is not a universal law that all intellectual history moves through discrete paradigms. His preface acknowledges Koyré, Metzger, Maier and Fleck as distinct resources. The later distinction between shared disciplinary commitments and exemplary solutions makes “paradigm” more precise. In his 1970 exchange, Kuhn stresses substantial agreement with Popper while distinguishing tests of puzzle solutions from challenges to basic theory. Popper accepts that normal research exists but disputes its educational desirability; Lakatos later proposes appraisal of research programmes through novel predictions. Their accusations of irrationalism are criticisms of Kuhn, not his own stated position. Skinner, Dunn and deMause use Kuhn for different historical purposes.
kuhn.representative_figures_and_works: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962; expanded second edition 1970). Distinguish his analysis of scientific communities from loose uses of paradigm to mean any school of historical writing. Read the 1962 preface alongside the 1969 postscript included in the second edition: sources of the argument and later clarification are different evidence.

rodney.label: Walter Rodney
rodney.description: Explains underdevelopment through historically unequal relations of slavery, colonial extraction and capitalism. Regional African research, Guyanese labor history and popular education give his work distinct scales and audiences. His account of systemic constraints also investigates changing societies; dependency analysis captures only part of his scholarship and politics.
rodney.representative_figures_and_works: The Groundings with My Brothers (1969); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972).
rodney.scope_note: A History of the Upper Guinea Coast, 1545–1800 (1970, from a 1966 thesis) reconstructs regional change; The Groundings with My Brothers (1969) concerns political education; How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972) offers a didactic synthesis. A History of the Guyanese Working People, 1881–1905 (posthumous, 1981) examines labor and racial divisions. His 1975 Marxism lecture distinguishes method from fixed European conclusions. James’s later strategic criticism coexists with formative intellectual exchange.

clr_james.label: C. L. R. James
clr_james.description: Places enslaved people’s revolutionary action at the center of the Haitian Revolution and reworks Marxist historical explanation through the Caribbean. His writing also investigates colonial society, race, and cultural life through cricket and autobiography.
clr_james.representative_figures_and_works: The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963); Beyond a Boundary (1963). The two editions of The Black Jacobins should not be treated as an unchanged argument.
clr_james.scope_note: The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963) and the 1971 lectures distinguish successive historical perspectives. James later sought closer study of rank-and-file leaders and praised Du Bois’s attention to political imagination. His recollections identify Trotsky, Lenin and Marx among resources, alongside Caribbean projects. Beyond a Boundary (1963) examines social divisions through clubs and treats cricket as an art. These connections do not make him a disciple of postwar British social history.

eric_williams.label: Eric Williams
eric_williams.description: Argues that slavery and slave-trade wealth contributed to British capitalist development, and that changing economic interests helped explain abolition. These are related but distinguishable theses whose mechanisms, timing, and weight remain debated. His work challenges accounts centered on European benevolence.
eric_williams.representative_figures_and_works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944). Distinguish the original book from later editions and from subsequent arguments about capitalism and slavery.
eric_williams.scope_note: The 1944 preface separates slavery’s contribution to industrial finance from industrial capitalism’s role in abolition; the conclusion gives economic forces explanatory priority. Williams names Ragatz, Pitman, Herskovits, Burch and Harlow among scholarly helpers. Drescher’s 1977 challenge concerns decline and the 1807 slave-trade abolition, not a refutation of every slavery/capitalism claim. From Columbus to Castro (1970) is a later Caribbean synthesis, here checked only bibliographically.

strands.title: Genealogy, values and historical explanation
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s critique asks both how moral judgments arise and what they are worth; Rée and Schopenhauer are distinct interlocutors. Origin and later function must not be conflated.

strands.title: Rhetoric, reference and historical achievement
strands.focus: Barthes analyzes the presentation of reality; Bann uses that analysis while questioning its scope and preserving source-based scrutiny. Formal analysis alone does not decide a historical claim’s truth.

strands.title: The historian, surviving sources and the historical picture
strands.focus: Michelet’s account of reciprocal formation and Huizinga’s warning about surviving art raise different questions about historical knowledge; they do not deny the need for evidence.

strands.title: Evidence, understanding and the historical question
strands.focus: Droysen, Dilthey, Croce and Collingwood offer different accounts of what inquiry does with traces, thought, context and practical concerns. These are explicit conceptual resources, not a common doctrine or a proved genealogy of later debate.

strands.title: Language use and following rules
strands.focus: Wittgenstein examines varied activities and similarities rather than one essence of language. Following a rule involves a practice; an interpretation cannot supply its own application without limit.

strands.title: Knowing how, action and accomplishment
strands.focus: Ryle distinguishes competent action from both an automatic movement and a performance governed by an endless series of prior theoretical decisions. A richer action description identifies purpose and circumstances.
strands.works: The Concept of Mind, II.1–3; The Thinking of Thoughts

strands.title: Narrative and historical understanding
strands.focus: White identifies particular philosophical interlocutors rather than responding to one undifferentiated philosophy of history.

strands.title: Laws, probability and explanation sketches
strands.focus: Hempel’s demand for testable relations permits incomplete research proposals and probabilistic accounts.

strands.title: Action and the limits of one explanatory model
strands.focus: Dray’s challenge includes reasons, uniqueness and pragmatic questions; it is not a ban on all generalization.
strands.works: Laws and Explanation (1957); Nature of Historical Explanation (1952)

strands.title: Selection, relevance and revisable interpretation
strands.focus: Becker and Carr preserve evidence while disputing self-interpreting facts; they do not offer identical positions.

strands.title: Historical craft, imagination and instruction
strands.focus: Elton’s research/writing/teaching agenda and Skinner’s apprenticeship reading identify practices of training.

strands.title: Narrative comprehension and truth
strands.focus: Mink separates grasping relations from truth tests and disputes both Gallie’s following and Hardy’s lived-narrative account.

strands.title: Knowledge of the past and speculative historical systems
strands.focus: Walsh’s scope distinguishes questions about inquiry from philosophies of the whole historical process.

frankfurt.label: Frankfurt School / critical theory
frankfurt.description: Critical theorists draw differently on Marx, Weber, and Freud to examine domination, culture, and rationality. Benjamin’s reflections on historical time and Habermas’s public sphere offer distinct resources for historians. Benjamin’s association with the Institute and Habermas’s later work should not imply a single institutional position or doctrine.

practice.label: Practice theory

Bourdieu’s habitus and strategies, de Certeau’s tactics, and Sewell’s account of structure offer different ways to connect agency, constraint, and meaning. culturalstudies.label: British cultural studies
culturalstudies.description: Examines culture as lived and contested, including popular forms, class, media, race, and gender. Debates among culturalist, structuralist, feminist, and antiracist projects reshape the field. It exchanges ideas with historical scholarship while retaining distinct institutional and disciplinary histories.

technology.label: History of technology
technology.description: Studies technological systems, invention, maintenance, use, and social change. Develops distinct institutions while exchanging questions with histories of science, economy, environment, and gender. Systems approaches and feminist studies of household technology show the range of its explanations. Wajcman’s feminist social-shaping questions and Bray’s Chinese domestic technologies broaden the field’s material and geographical examples.

ivy_pinchbeck.label: Ivy Pinchbeck
ivy_pinchbeck.description: Reconstructs women’s work before and during industrialization through household production, wages, training and agricultural change. She emphasizes unequal disruption while arguing for eventual benefits, a position distinct from Clark’s account of capitalist development.
ivy_pinchbeck.representative_figures_and_works: Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution, 1750–1850 (1930; new preface in the 1969 reprint). The original preface acknowledges Eileen Power’s direction of the research and Lilian Knowles’s earlier guidance.
ivy_pinchbeck.scope_note: The complete 1930 introduction distinguishes paid visibility from productive work itself and separates married women, single women and workers supporting families. Power directs the acknowledged research; Knowles gives early guidance and Dorothy George supplies specific evidence. The 1969 preface, signed 1968, calls for later occupational research without supplying it. The broad optimistic conclusion remains an attributed argument; most occupational chapters and the original conclusion are unread.

alice_clark.label: Alice Clark
alice_clark.description: Studies women’s paid and unpaid production through overlapping household and capitalist arrangements. Differences of class and marital position shape her account of changing work, training and authority; her chronology and assumptions about earlier households remain contested.
alice_clark.representative_figures_and_works: Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919). Compare with Pinchbeck’s later-period study to examine how historians explain the relationship between economic change and women’s autonomy.
alice_clark.scope_note: The 1919 preface credits Schreiner, Knowles and Power’s unpublished research. Introduction and conclusion distinguish production for use, family enterprise and individual wages, while admitting conjectural medieval comparisons and incomplete causal evidence. Maternal and racial assumptions belong to Clark’s historical position. Erickson’s 1992 introduction values unpaid-work analysis while disputing chronology and household equality. Main occupational cases are not newly read; neither timeless equality nor a uniform decline for all women is established.

mary_ritter_beard.label: Mary Ritter Beard
mary_ritter_beard.description: Argues that women helped make historical institutions and events, and that histories must investigate their activity rather than assume universal passivity. Her work combines historical argument, collaborative synthesis and efforts to preserve and teach women’s records.
mary_ritter_beard.representative_figures_and_works: Woman as Force in History: A Study in Traditions and Realities (1946); work supporting women’s documentary collections, including the Sophia Smith Collection. Her account of agency remains open to criticism about differences among women and structures of power.
mary_ritter_beard.scope_note: Woman as Force in History (1946) challenges the subject-sex tradition through legal and other historical inquiry; its preface does not establish that agency cancels subordination. WCWA (1935–1940) and Smith collecting depended on Schwimmer, Grierson, donors and other collaborators. Voss-Hubbard documents Black women’s limited authority and funding within WCWA. Cott’s 1991 editorial recovery uses letters preserved by correspondents. Mary’s distinct work coexists with collaboration with Charles; legal cases and specific later theoretical criticism remain to be checked.

julia_cherry_spruill.label: Julia Cherry Spruill
julia_cherry_spruill.date_label: Women’s social history in colonial America · 1938
julia_cherry_spruill.description: Investigates women’s everyday life, institutions, work and public activity in the colonial South through varied documentary evidence. Later reissues and public interpretation renew use of her work while exposing limits in whose lives become sustained research questions.
julia_cherry_spruill.representative_figures_and_works: Women’s Life and Work in the Southern Colonies (1938); later reissues associated with Anne Firor Scott show that the field’s expansion also involved renewed attention to earlier scholarship.
julia_cherry_spruill.scope_note: Richter’s complete 1999 review mediates Spruill’s shift from attitudes to empirical groundwork and her distinction between prescribed reading and actual behavior. The book examines status and regional differences, but mentions Black and Native women without sustained questions about their life and work, in Richter’s assessment. Scott’s 1972 and 1998 introductions are editorial reception; Colonial Williamsburg use is documented, while Richter’s own proposed slavery research remains an intention. Earlier methods are not membership in postwar social history, and friendship with Beard does not prove transmission.

lucy_maynard_salmon.label: Lucy Maynard Salmon
lucy_maynard_salmon.description: Brings domestic employment, everyday evidence and critical teaching into historical inquiry. Domestic Service combines questionnaires, statistical comparison and historical explanation, treating household work as connected to wider economic change. Her practice depends on respondents, students, librarians and statistical collaborators.
lucy_maynard_salmon.representative_figures_and_works: Domestic Service (1897); teaching and research at Vassar, including work with cookbooks and household material evidence. Connects histories of women’s work to a wider reconsideration of what counts as a historical source.
lucy_maynard_salmon.scope_note: The 1897 preface and opening chapters explain response limits and distinguish facts from proposed remedies; the 1901 edition adds European inquiry. Distribution through college and association networks is not established probability sampling, despite Salmon’s claim to representativeness. barbara_tuchman.label: Barbara W. Tuchman
barbara_tuchman.description: Builds historical narratives around decisions, personalities and political circumstances, combining readable prose with documentary reconstruction. Her accounts of research identify specialist help, conflicting evidence and uncertain inference. Critical reception asks how narrative selection relates to wider social and institutional explanation.
barbara_tuchman.representative_figures_and_works: The Guns of August (1962). A useful case for asking how narrative pace, characterization, and the selection of events support or constrain an explanation.
barbara_tuchman.scope_note: The Guns of August (1962) precedes the 1979 revival diagnosis. In “In Search of History” Tuchman explicitly invokes Ranke’s historical truth and Bowen’s reader principle while rejecting invented detail. A Distant Mirror (1978) uses Coucy as a narrative vehicle and acknowledges an unanswered initial causal question, selection bias and debts to editors, chroniclers and sociological medievalists. Stone’s 1978 criticism and Fox-Genovese’s defense are distinct interpretations, not a simple narrative-versus-analysis divide. Specialist assistance does not mean agreement with every conclusion; Tuchman is not placed in women’s history solely because she is a woman, or in Marxism because a Marxist defended her.

ep_thompson.label: E. P. Thompson
ep_thompson.description: Makes culture, experience, and agency central to the historical formation of class, contributing to an early cultural reorientation within Marxist social history. He retained materialist explanation while disputing other uses of culture and theory. Feminist historians developed resources from his work while criticizing its handling of gender; he resisted some of their extensions and criticisms. This is an intertwined history of inheritance and disagreement, not a simple replacement of class by culture.
ep_thompson.representative_figures_and_works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); The Poverty of Theory, or an Orrery of Errors (1978). Edward Palmer Thompson has an individual entry here alongside Dorothy Thompson, whose research and arguments remain distinct.

Dorothy’s intellectual contribution is acknowledged in the Making preface; their separate authorship and reciprocal collaboration remain distinct. eric_hobsbawm.label: Eric Hobsbawm
eric_hobsbawm.date_label: Primitive Rebels 1959 · The Age of… 1962–1994 · The Invention of Tradition 1983 · Budapest lecture 1993 · Interesting Times 2002 · How to Change the World 2011 · Fractured Times 2013
eric_hobsbawm.description: A historian of labour, popular protest, capitalist transformation and nations, who studies cultural evidence and explanatory synthesis across different scales; his responses to criticism revise some claims while retaining others. After Primitive Rebels (1959) and Labouring Men (1964), his four Age of… volumes (1962–1994) became, for reviewers, a synthesis of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991; Tony Judt called The Age of Capital his greatest work and criticised The Age of Extremes for keeping the political categories of the 1930s (1995). With Terence Ranger he edited The Invention of Tradition (1983); in a 1993 lecture in Budapest he told historians to resist national myths as they formed and to hold to the difference between fact and fiction. Later books include On History (1997); the memoir Interesting Times (2002), which Perry Anderson read as a fifth volume of the same project: he finds in its explanation of remaining Communist after 1956 what most readers would see as integrity, while faulting its limited engagement with the political history of European Communism and its treatment of other Marxists; How to Change the World (2011), a history of Marxism, which Terry Eagleton credits with judiciousness while criticising its handling of ideas, including Althusser, feminism and Trotskyism; and the posthumous Fractured Times (2013).
eric_hobsbawm.representative_figures_and_works: Primitive Rebels (1959); The Age of Revolution (1962); Labouring Men (1964); Industry and Empire (1968); Bandits (1969; revised 2000); The Age of Capital (1975); response to Stone on narrative (1980); with Terence Ranger, The Invention of Tradition (1983); The Age of Empire (1987); Nations and Nationalism since 1780 (1990); “The New Threat to History” (1993); The Age of Extremes (1994); On History (1997); Interesting Times (2002); Globalisation, Democracy and Terrorism (2007); How to Change the World (2011); Fractured Times (2013). Readings: Judt (1995); Anderson (2002); Black (2003–4); Eagleton (2011); Morgan (2013); Mayer on Evans’s biography (2020).
eric_hobsbawm.scope_note: The 1980 narrative reply, Bandits in its revised 2000 form, and Nations and Nationalism (1990/1992) distinguish debate, self-revision and historical synthesis. Later concessions about myth and political power are not projected into 1969. Colombian interlocutors and European comparative models supply named resources. Labouring Men and the main nationalism cases remain unread; selected primary support does not audit his entire career or generalizations. The 1993 Budapest lecture is read in full. The Age of… volumes, Primitive Rebels, Industry and Empire, On History, Interesting Times, How to Change the World and Fractured Times are unread here; they are dated and characterised through named readers (Judt, Anderson, Black, Eagleton, Morgan, the Guardian obituarists, and Mayer on Evans’s 2019 biography). No reception of The Invention of Tradition or of Nations and Nationalism is read here: the 1983 volume rests on its publisher record and the 1990 book on its preview, and Judt’s review and the 1993 lecture do not supply that reception. Criticism of individual contributors to the 1983 volume is not criticism of Hobsbawm’s conceptual programme.

roger_chartier.label: Roger Chartier
roger_chartier.date_label: Lectures et lecteurs 1987 · Le monde comme représentation 1989 · Les origines culturelles 1990 · questions to White 1993 · “La nouvelle histoire culturelle existe-t-elle ?” 2003 · Collège de France 2007–2016 · Cardenio 2011 · Éditer et traduire 2021
roger_chartier.description: A historian of reading, the book and written culture in early modern Europe who explains how textual forms, reading practices and collective representations shape social differences. His programme, set out in “Le monde comme représentation” (1989), joins material bibliography to differentiated appropriation, critically reworks Annales and uses conceptual resources without accepting every formulation. In 1993 he put four questions to Hayden White, on language, tropology, the procedures of research and relativism before the Shoah; they are known here through White’s 1995 rejoinder. In 2003 he argued that practices cannot be reduced to discourse, doubted that the new cultural history was as coherent as Lynn Hunt had claimed, and described it as a space of debate that had moved away from “the illusions of the linguistic turn”. He held the Collège de France chair “Écrit et cultures dans l’Europe moderne” from 2007 to 2016; his inaugural lecture called the tide of digital textuality a major rupture in the history of written culture, as his reviewer Christian Jouhaud quotes it. Later books, known here through their reviewers, follow the mobility of texts: the lost play Cardenio between Cervantes and Shakespeare (2011) and Éditer et traduire (2021).
roger_chartier.representative_figures_and_works: Lectures et lecteurs dans la France d’Ancien Régime (1987); “Le monde comme représentation” (1989); Les origines culturelles de la Révolution française (1990; English 1991); L’ordre des livres (1992; English 1994); “Quatre questions à Hayden White” (1993); On the Edge of the Cliff (1996); « La nouvelle histoire culturelle existe-t-elle ? » (2003); Inscrire et effacer (2005); Écouter les morts avec les yeux (Collège de France inaugural lecture, 2007); Cardenio entre Cervantès et Shakespeare (2011); The Author’s Hand and the Printer’s Mind (2013); Éditer et traduire (2021). Readings: White (1995); Jouhaud (2008, 2022); Boucheron (2014).
roger_chartier.scope_note: The 1989 article explicitly engages McKenzie, Ricœur, Fish, Marin, Durkheim/Mauss, Elias, Ginzburg, Certeau and Foucault. Productive Foucault use coexists with a different account of appropriation; criticism of Braudel concerns an explanatory hierarchy. Social divisions include gender, generation, religion and education as well as class. The primary article is checked, but its cited works and historical examples do not thereby receive independent verification. Later work: the 2003 article is read in full; the 1993 questions to White are known only through White’s 1995 rejoinder, read in its authorised Portuguese translation; the 2007 dialogue with Darnton is read in part in Portuguese translation. The books listed here are unread unless an excerpt is separately identified: dates come from the Prismas bibliography (2022) and publisher pages, and their arguments from named reviewers (Jouhaud, Boucheron); Inscrire et effacer is listed bibliographically only. Boucheron’s expectation that medievalists will dispute his dating of the author function is an anticipated objection, not a controversy investigated here. The 1998 French Historical Studies forum is dated from metadata only, and the 1985–88 exchange with Robert Darnton is unread; neither is covered substantively.

urbanhistory.label: Urban history
urbanhistory.date_label: Earlier city histories · postwar expansion · Urban History Yearbook 1974
urbanhistory.description: Studies cities and urbanization through institutions, populations, built environments and connections beyond city boundaries. urbanhistory.scope_note: British institution-building and US quantitative urban studies do not define one school or exhaust the field. Cities are not self-contained units. Delhi adds a specific colonial inquiry; wider Asian, African, Latin American and medieval/early-modern historiographies remain underrepresented. Journal milestones mark consolidation, not the first historical study of cities.

spatialhistory.date_label: Sauer 1925 · Hoskins 1955 · critical spatial studies and historical GIS by the 1990s

intellectualhistory.label: Intellectual history
intellectualhistory.date_label: Earlier histories of thought · Lovejoy 1936 · Skinner 1969 · plural programmes through the 1990s
intellectualhistory.description: Studies thought, concepts, arguments and their production, circulation and interpretation in historical settings. History of ideas, contextual political thought, conceptual history, textual criticism and the material history of publishing supply overlapping but disputed methods. Intellectual history extends beyond the Cambridge School and beyond a canon of European philosophers.

Pocock: “The history of political thought” (1962); The Machiavellian Moment (1975); Annabel S. Brett: Liberty, Right and Nature (1997); Reinhart Koselleck: Futures Past (German 1979; English 1985); Dominick LaCapra: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983); John E. Toews: “Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn” (1987); Robert Darnton: The Business of Enlightenment (1979); Masao Maruyama: Studies in the Intellectual History of Tokugawa Japan (essays 1940–1944; English 1974); Mikiso Hane: English translation of Maruyama’s Studies (1974).

intellectualhistory.scope_note: An enduring field with internal disagreements, not a single lineage from Lovejoy to contextualism. The existing Cambridge School and Conceptual history entries retain their specificity. Maruyama supplies one Japanese inquiry with explicit translation credit, not global representation or evidence of Cambridge influence. Social and cultural settings matter without reducing texts to reflections of social position. Women’s intellectual histories and African, Islamic, South Asian and Latin American traditions still need much fuller coverage.

strands.title: History of ideas and recurring concepts
strands.focus: Lovejoy follows changing combinations of ideas across philosophical, religious and literary materials.

strands.title: Arguments, languages and historical action
strands.focus: Skinner, Pocock and Brett pursue distinct contextual inquiries; they are not interchangeable statements of one method.

strands.title: Conceptual change and historical time
strands.focus: Koselleck relates semantic change to social history without making concepts and social structures identical.

strands.title: Texts, contexts and experience
strands.focus: LaCapra develops textual criticism; Toews’s titled intervention marks a related debate whose detailed claims remain a reading task.

strands.title: Publishing and the circulation of ideas
strands.focus: Darnton connects thought with the material and commercial work of producing and distributing books. Chartier’s later studies follow texts’ mobility across attributions, printed versions, genres and translations, in his reviewers’ accounts.

strands.title: Japanese political thought and translation
strands.focus: Maruyama’s Tokugawa studies and Hane’s translation widen the selection while leaving its modernization interpretation open to scrutiny.

labourhistory.label: Labour history
labourhistory.date_label: Webbs 1894/1920 · Thompson 1963 · expanding comparative and feminist inquiries in the 1970s–1990s
labourhistory.description: Studies work, workers, labour relations and collective organisation across paid, unpaid, coerced, agricultural and industrial settings. Labour history includes unions and politics, workplace authority, household economies, culture, race, gender and colonial categories. Labour and labor are spelling variants; neither social history nor British Marxism exhausts the field.

labourhistory.scope_note: Institutional histories, Marxist cultural analysis, feminist inquiry and colonial labour studies coexist and disagree. Thompson’s work already contains a cultural reorientation; later gender analysis involves productive inheritance as well as criticism. This selection includes Britain, the United States, France, South Asia and Africa but does not constitute global coverage. Labour institutions and historical scholarship about them have different chronologies. Fuller Latin American, Caribbean, East Asian and Indigenous labour historiographies remain priorities.

ethnohistory.date_label: Earlier interdisciplinary work · Great Lakes–Ohio Valley project 1953 · Lurie 1961 · continuing regional programmes
ethnohistory.description: Combines historical and anthropological inquiry through archives, material evidence, language, oral traditions and situated cultural interpretation. North American claims research, Wendat/Huron historical reconstruction, Nahua documentary studies and Andean historical anthropology form distinct programmes. Ethnohistory studies historical change rather than assigning some peoples to an unchanging ethnographic past.

ethnohistory.scope_note: The field overlaps with Indigenous history but does not automatically confer Indigenous authority, community consent or decolonizing method. Claims research could serve governments as well as claimants. Indigenous authors appear here as qualified interlocutors and critics, not as members of an externally assigned school. Lurie herself disputes restricting the approach to particular peoples. The Americas dominate this initial selection; Vansina provides a comparison with African oral-tradition methodology, not proof that African history descends from US ethnohistory.
