joan_wallach_scott.label: Joan Wallach Scott
joan_wallach_scott.date_label: Women’s work 1975 · Gender 1986 · Experience 1991 · Only Paradoxes 1996 · Parité! 2005 · The Politics of the Veil 2007 · “Unanswered Questions” 2008 · Sex and Secularism 2017 · On the Judgment of History 2020
joan_wallach_scott.description: A historian of modern France who, after studies of women’s work and the family with Louise Tilly (1975, 1978), proposed gender as a historical analysis of social relationships and power (1986), connecting symbols, normative claims, institutions and subjectivity while insisting on historical variation, and questioned experience as self-evident evidence (1991). Gender and the Politics of History (1988) made her, in Laura Lee Downs’s words, “the spokesperson for gender history”; Palmer, Valverde and Downs contested her poststructuralism. Later books, presented here through their reviewers, trace French feminists’ paradoxes between the abstract individual and sexual difference (Only Paradoxes to Offer, 1996, as Landes reads it), the parity movement (Parité!, 2005, as Dean reads it), the headscarf ban (The Politics of the Veil, 2007, as Laborde reads it) and gender in the discourse of secularism (Sex and Secularism, 2017, as Whitney and O’Grady read it); Laborde finds the veil book’s normative premises unclear, and O’Grady objects that the later book holds nineteenth-century Europeans to present moral standards. In a 2018 interview Scott asked how to write a critique of secularism without rejecting it. Answering an AHR forum on her 1986 essay (2008), she insisted that gender is useful only as a question and explained her use of psychoanalysis and fantasy to keep it critical; her reply presents the forum’s reception as geographically and politically situated, quoting Heidi Tinsman, and disputes Joanne Meyerowitz’s reading of a change of direction, asserting continuity in her concern with sexual difference. With Ethan Kleinberg and Gary Wilder she called for a theorized “critical history” (2018); Knowledge, Power, and Academic Freedom (2019), in Robin Whitaker’s account, treats academic freedom as an ethical practice and holds that disciplinary practice is no power-free zone; she has also written on the claim that history will judge (2020).
joan_wallach_scott.representative_figures_and_works: “Women’s Work and the Family in Nineteenth-Century Europe” (with Louise Tilly, 1975); Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis (1986); “On Language, Gender, and Working-Class History” (1987); Gender and the Politics of History (1988; revised 1999; 2018); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Only Paradoxes to Offer (1996); “The ‘Class’ We Have Lost” (2000); Parité! (2005); The Politics of the Veil (2007); “Unanswered Questions” (2008); The Fantasy of Feminist History (2011); “The Incommensurability of Psychoanalysis and History” (2012); Sex and Secularism (2017); Theses on Theory and History (with Kleinberg and Wilder, 2018); Knowledge, Power, and Academic Freedom (2019); On the Judgment of History (2020). Readings: Valverde (1990); Downs (1993); Landes (1997); Dean (2006); Laborde (2008); the AHR forum (2008); Whitney and O’Grady (2018); Whitaker (2019); McLemee (2020).
joan_wallach_scott.scope_note: Existing cross-field presence warrants a visible argument, not just another name in a roster. The 1986 and 1991 interventions and the 1987 forum reply are read in her own words; “Unanswered Questions” (2008) is read in full in an authorised Spanish translation, so its wording is not given as her English. The books from Only Paradoxes to Offer (1996) to On the Judgment of History (2020) are unread here and are characterised through named reviewers (Landes, Dean, Laborde, Whitney, O’Grady, Whitaker, McLemee) and publisher descriptions; the 2000 and 2012 articles through their abstracts. The AHR forum contributions (2008) are unread: Tinsman and Meyerowitz appear only as Scott’s reply quotes or reports them. Secularism and academic freedom have no entries of their own, so those arguments appear in the description and timeline; the veil and secularism books are drawn as a contribution to postcolonial critique.

natalie_zemon_davis.label: Natalie Zemon Davis
natalie_zemon_davis.date_label: “The Reasons of Misrule” 1971 · “The Rites of Violence” 1973 · Society and Culture in Early Modern France 1975 · “Women’s History in Transition” 1976 · The Return of Martin Guerre 1982–83 · Fiction in the Archives 1987 · Women on the Margins 1995 · Slaves on Screen and The Gift 2000 · Trickster Travels 2006
natalie_zemon_davis.description: A historian of sixteenth-century France whose work moved from the social history of Lyon’s printing workers to ritual, gender, storytelling and lives that crossed religious and colonial borders. By her own account (1997) she ‘combined archival work with the study of printed texts of multiple genres’, and Laurie Nussdorfer’s memorial calls her ‘the rare social historian who valued printed sources’. In ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973) she argued that religious riot drew on ‘a store of punitive or purificatory traditions’ and had ‘a connection in time, place and form with the life of worship’, so that such violence was ‘related here less to the pathological than to the normal’; she explicitly distinguished explaining the ritual structure of violence from granting a right to commit it: ‘the rites of violence are not the rights of violence in any absolute sense’. She acknowledged the crowd histories of Rudé, Hobsbawm, Thompson and Tilly and applied Thompson’s account of the food riot’s legitimation to the religious crowd. By her own account she came to ritual through Van Gennep’s folklore and read Evans-Pritchard, Turner, Geertz and Mintz ‘eclectically … not looking for solutions, but for questions’ (1997); Thompson, for his part, called her charivari essay ‘une étude importante’ (1972). Joan Scott (1986) quoted her call to study ‘the history of both women and men’ as an early relational use of gender, and with Jill Conway she taught in 1971 what she called ‘the first course in women’s history in Canada’. In 1997 she said she came to microhistory, ‘or what I called ethnography’, through the film of Martin Guerre, on whose script she worked; her book followed in French (1982) and English (1983). Robert Finlay (1988) charged that she had ‘permitted an excess of invention’ against ‘the sovereignty of the sources’; she answered that where reconstruction stops and invention begins was ‘precisely the question I hoped readers would ask’. In her 1997 retrospect she described the ‘fiction’ of Fiction in the Archives (1987) as ‘the crafting element’, not falsification, and Women on the Margins (1995) as ‘a decentered comparison’ of three lives, whose conclusion keeps religious difference and colonial domination in view. The Holberg committee (2010) described The Gift (2000) as illuminating ‘the intricate forms of pre-market exchange and reciprocity’, Slaves on Screen (2000) as dealing with ‘the alteration of historical material in contemporary film’ and Trickster Travels (2006), with Women on the Margins, as exploring ‘the translation and transmission of cultures’; it saw her uniqueness in ‘connecting early modern Europe with new areas of comparative history’.
natalie_zemon_davis.representative_figures_and_works: Natalie Zemon Davis (1928–2023); dissertation on Lyon’s Protestants and printing workers (1959); “A Trade Union in Sixteenth-Century France” (Economic History Review, 1966); “The Reasons of Misrule: Youth Groups and Charivaris in Sixteenth-Century France” (Past and Present, 1971); “The Rites of Violence: Religious Riot in Sixteenth-Century France” (Past and Present, 1973; reprinted in Society and Culture in Early Modern France, 1975); “‘Women’s History’ in Transition: The European Case” (Feminist Studies, 1976; quoted by Scott, 1986); Le Retour de Martin Guerre (Paris: Robert Laffont, 1982; the catalogue record also credits Jean-Claude Carrière and Daniel Vigne, scenarist and director of the 1982 film on whose script she worked) and The Return of Martin Guerre (Harvard, 1983); “History’s Two Bodies” (AHA presidential address, 1987; AHR 1988); Fiction in the Archives: Pardon Tales and Their Tellers in Sixteenth-Century France (1987); “On the Lame” (AHR Forum, 1988, reply to Finlay); Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (1995); A Life of Learning (Haskins Lecture, 1997); Slaves on Screen: Film and Historical Vision (2000); The Gift in Sixteenth-Century France (2000); Trickster Travels: A Sixteenth-Century Muslim between Worlds (2006); “Decentering History” (Holberg Symposium, 2010); later titles named in Nussdorfer’s memorial (unread): Leo Africanus Discovers Comedy: Theatre and Poetry Across the Mediterranean (2021) and Listening to the Languages of the People: Lazare Sainéan on Romanian, Yiddish and French (2022). Readers and critics: E. P. Thompson (1972); Lawrence Stone (1979); Joan Scott (1986); Robert Finlay (1988); Lynn Hunt, ed., with Suzanne Desan’s chapter (1989); Judith Jackson Fossett (2001); Holberg Prize committee (2010); Alexandra Walsham (2017); Laurie Nussdorfer (2023); Carla Hesse (2024).
natalie_zemon_davis.scope_note: Read for revision 1.143: ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973), pp. 52–53, 57, 60–61 and 90–91; her Haskins Lecture, A Life of Learning (1997), in full, cited as her later account of her course, not as evidence of what the earlier works say; ‘On the Lame’ (1988), pp. 572, 574–576, 584, 587, 600 and 602–603; Finlay’s critique (1988) in full; Stone (1979), pp. 3 and 18; Scott (1986), p. 1054; and, earlier, the prologue, conclusion and acknowledgments of Women on the Margins. Thompson’s ‘Rough Music’ (1972, by paragraph in a 2020 reprint), her AHA address (1987) and the AHA memorial (2024) are read only in short excerpts. The Return of Martin Guerre, Fiction in the Archives, The Gift, Slaves on Screen, Trickster Travels and the 2021–22 books are unread: they supply bibliographic dates and mediated interpretations only, given in her own retrospect or in named readers’ words (the Holberg committee, Fossett, Finlay, Nussdorfer). Also unread: ‘Women’s History in Transition’ (1976; her words as Scott quotes them), Estèbe’s 1975 comment on ‘Rites’ and her rejoinder, Ginzburg’s 1984 postface to the Italian Martin Guerre, Desan’s 1989 chapter and the Davis–Thompson letters (Walsham 2017; opening only). She is not presented as the founder of microhistory, cultural history or gender history: by her own account Le Roy Ladurie and Ginzburg reached microhistory by other routes, Scott quotes her as one relational voice among others, and anthropology supplied questions tested on ‘only historical evidence’. Finlay’s charge of invention and her reply are both kept, as is Fossett’s criticism (2001) that Slaves on Screen ‘raises more questions than it answers’. Not to be confused with J. C. Davis (the Ranter debate) or Donald F. Davis (Canadian urban history).

lynn_hunt.label: Lynn Hunt
lynn_hunt.date_label: Politics, Culture, and Class 1984 · The New Cultural History 1989 · Telling the Truth about History 1994 · AHA address 2003 · Inventing Human Rights 2007 · Writing History in the Global Era 2014
lynn_hunt.description: A historian of the French Revolution whose Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984) joined revolutionary symbols and rhetoric to the sociology of political actors, using Geertz’s interpretive frame, and whose introduction to The New Cultural History (1989) reassessed the explanatory models of social history, recognising turns toward culture within Marxist and Annales histories while questioning the priority assigned to social experience. With Joyce Appleby and Margaret Jacob she defended a “practical realism” (1994), and with Victoria Bonnell she edited Beyond the Cultural Turn (1999). In her AHA presidential address (2003) she asked how the Revolution could “produce such contradictory consequences” as terror, democracy and human rights. Inventing Human Rights (2007), which reviewers summarise as tracing rights to imagined empathy, novels and the rejection of torture, was contested by Samuel Moyn and David A. Bell. Writing History in the Global Era (2014), the book around which this atlas was first developed, argued, in her reviewer’s summary, that globalization had become a new paradigm that could wash away the gains of cultural history.
lynn_hunt.representative_figures_and_works: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984); Introduction: History, Culture, and Text, in The New Cultural History (1989), editor; The Family Romance of the French Revolution (1992); with Joyce Appleby and Margaret Jacob, Telling the Truth about History (1994); with Victoria Bonnell, Beyond the Cultural Turn (1999); “The World We Have Gained: The Future of the French Revolution” (AHA presidential address, 2003); Inventing Human Rights (2007); Writing History in the Global Era (2014). Readings: Moyn (2007); Bell (2007); McClure (2015).
lynn_hunt.scope_note: Connects the cultural turn to disputes within social explanation. Hunt authored the 1989 introduction and edited the collection; she did not author all its essays. Her political-culture work rests on the existing reading of the 1984 book’s chapter openings, and her later revolution argument on the 2003 address read through the AHA web text. Inventing Human Rights and Writing History in the Global Era are presented through their reviewers (Moyn, Bell, McClure); the books themselves are unread here. The atlas’s Identity histories grouping is her later classification and does not make her its founder. No human-rights entry exists; the 2007 book is drawn as a contribution to cultural history and as the object of a critique.

catherine_hall.label: Catherine Hall
catherine_hall.date_label: Family Fortunes 1987 · White, Male and Middle Class 1992 · Defining the Victorian Nation 2000 · Civilising Subjects 2002 · Legacies of British Slave-ownership 2009– · Macaulay and Son 2012 · Lucky Valley 2024
catherine_hall.description: A historian of gender, class, race and empire. With Leonore Davidoff she related English middle-class formation to gender, family, religion and economic life in Family Fortunes (1987), investigating class identities and gender relations together rather than in separate accounts. Civilising Subjects (2002), whose “central argument”, she wrote, “is that being a colonizer was part of the construction of Englishness”, followed Birmingham abolitionists and Baptist missionaries to Jamaica; she credited C. L. R. James with showing what can be gained by studying “metropole and colony in one lens”. Angela Woollacott (2006) reads it as postcolonial history for its “insistence on the interconstitutive connections between colony and metropole”, and Edward Said (2003) praised it while asking for subaltern voices. From 2009 she led, with her research associates Nicholas Draper and Keith McClelland, University College London’s Legacies of British Slave-ownership project, tracing the slave-owners compensated at emancipation into Victorian Britain. In 2014 she and her coauthors identified a move toward modified versions of Williams’s thesis among economic historians, and she argued, against the British Marxist historians’ neglect of “race, slavery and the Caribbean”, that gender and race shaped the formation of capital. Lucky Valley (2024) turns to Edward Long and “racial capitalism”.
catherine_hall.representative_figures_and_works: With Leonore Davidoff, Family Fortunes: Men and Women of the English Middle Class 1780–1850 (1987); White, Male and Middle Class (1992); with Keith McClelland and Jane Rendall, Defining the Victorian Nation (2000); Civilising Subjects: Metropole and Colony in the English Imagination, 1830–1867 (2002); Macaulay and Son: Architects of Imperial Britain (2012); with Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland, Katie Donington and Rachel Lang, Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014); “Gendering Property, Racing Capital” (History Workshop Journal, 2014); Lucky Valley: Edward Long and the History of Racial Capitalism (2024). Joint works; retain all coauthor credits. Readings: Said (2003); Gikandi, Levine and Holt (JBS, 2003, as Hall answers them); Woollacott (2006); Tao Wei (2014).
catherine_hall.scope_note: Equal coauthor credit with Davidoff for Family Fortunes, whose newly checked evidence is the indexed prologue abstract and publisher description of a later edition. Family Fortunes and her imperial and slavery work (2002–2014) are distinct projects linked by attention to gender, class and race. The Legacies of British Slave-ownership is collective work and its edges credit the team. Her 2014 History Workshop Journal essay is read in her own words; Civilising Subjects is presented through her own 2003 reply to its commentators (pp. 530–537, read by a second research pass), Said’s and Woollacott’s readings and its publisher description; the commentators’ own texts are unread; Legacies is read through its jointly written introduction in excerpts without print pages and UCL’s 2014 impact case study; Macaulay and Son through Tao Wei’s review; White, Male and Middle Class, Defining the Victorian Nation and Lucky Valley through contents or publisher descriptions only. She is not Stuart Hall.

lorraine_daston.label: Lorraine Daston
lorraine_daston.date_label: Classical Probability 1988 · The Image of Objectivity 1992 · The Moral Economy of Science 1995 · Objectivity 2007 · Science Studies and the History of Science 2009 · Rules 2022
lorraine_daston.description: A historian of science who historicizes the categories of scientific knowing. Her books include Classical Probability in the Enlightenment (1988) and, with Katharine Park, Wonders and the Order of Nature, 1150–1750 (1998). In “The Moral Economy of Science” (1995) she argued that certain forms of empiricism, quantification and objectivity “require moral economies”, “a web of affect-saturated values”, drawing on Elias’s civilizing process and distinguishing her sense of the term from E. P. Thompson’s. With Peter Galison she studied objectivity itself: their 1992 article distinguishes mechanical objectivity from other historically formed components of the concept, and their book Objectivity (2007) treats it, in reviewers’ readings, as one epistemic virtue beside others rather than their successor. She was a director at the Max Planck Institute for the History of Science from 1995 until 2019. In 2009 she argued that the history of science had become “a discipline” while science studies remained “undisciplined”, and that “to historicize the category of the fact, objectivity, or proof is not thereby to debunk it”.
lorraine_daston.representative_figures_and_works: Classical Probability in the Enlightenment (1988); with Peter Galison, “The Image of Objectivity” (1992); “The Moral Economy of Science” (1995); with Katharine Park, Wonders and the Order of Nature, 1150–1750 (1998); with Peter Galison, Objectivity (2007); “Science Studies and the History of Science” (2009); Rules: A Short History of What We Live By (2022). Joint works; retain all coauthor credits. Readings: Henning (2008); Switzer (2009); Lahav (2023).
lorraine_daston.scope_note: Adds a substantive history-of-science contribution beyond gender history. Galison retains equal authorship and argument credit for the 1992 article and the 2007 book, and Park for Wonders. Their historical analysis does not assert that scientific objectivity is simply impossible: in 2009 she wrote that “‘If historical, then relative’ is a non sequitur”. The 1995 and 2009 essays are read in her own words; Objectivity and Rules remain unread: their content is mediated by reviewers (Switzer and Henning; Lahav) and Rules by its publisher’s description, and the 1988 and 1998 books are dated from her 2009 author note and the Collège de France biography and carry no argument here. “Historical epistemology” in her sense is not the French tradition of the atlas’s Historical epistemology entry, and no edge connects them.

ian_mckay.label: Ian McKay
ian_mckay.date_label: Tartanism Triumphant 1992 · The Quest of the Folk 1994 · 'A Note on Region' and the liberal order prospectus 2000 · later readings 2005, 2008, 2009
ian_mckay.description: Reads twentieth-century Nova Scotia's 'folk' as a cultural selection by folklorists, handicraft planners, writers and the tourist state, and as a local version of an international antimodernist wave (1992, 1994). In 2000 he proposed treating Canada as a project of liberal rule, to be studied through the implantation of liberalism across a heterogeneous terrain, and asked how 'region' fits that project. Later work turns to the Canadian left as a counter-project (2005, 2008) and answers the framework's critics (2009).

Later readings: Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005); Reasoning Otherwise (2008); “Canada as a Long Liberal Revolution” (2009).

harold_a_innis.label: Harold A. Innis
harold_a_innis.date_label: The Fur Trade in Canada 1930 · The Cod Fisheries 1940 · Empire and Communications 1950 · The Bias of Communication 1951
harold_a_innis.description: A Toronto political economist whose staple studies read Canada's development through the export of raw materials to industrial centres in Britain and the United States. The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) concludes that 'the economic history of Canada has been dominated by the discrepancy between the center and the margin of western civilization', that the history of the fur trade is 'the history of contact between two civilizations', and that 'the present Dominion emerged not in spite of geography but because of it'. The Cod Fisheries (1940) follows a second staple as the history of an international economy. After 1940 he turned to the media of communication and empire (Empire and Communications, 1950; The Bias of Communication, 1951).
harold_a_innis.representative_figures_and_works: Harold A. Innis (1894–1952); The Fur Trade in Canada: An Introduction to Canadian Economic History (1930); The Cod Fisheries: The History of an International Economy (1940); Empire and Communications (1950); The Bias of Communication (1951; 1964 reissue with an introduction by Marshall McLuhan). Readings: Brady's memoir (1953); Watkins, “A Staple Theory of Economic Growth” (1963); Salmon (1997).
harold_a_innis.scope_note: This entry presents the staple studies. The Fur Trade in Canada is checked at its contents and its conclusion (pp. 386–397, read in a scan of the 1930 edition); The Cod Fisheries and the two communication books are checked at catalogue level, and the turn to communication rests on Brady's 1953 memoir. He is not presented as the originator of the staple approach. Watkins (1963) calls him its 'leading innovator' but adds that 'others tilled the same vineyard'. Salmon (1997) notes that 'Innis never claimed to have originated the staples theory', Brady names Adam Shortt 'the pioneer in these economic studies', and Mackintosh's 1923 article precedes the fur-trade book. The 1930 conclusion's statements about Indigenous peoples (their 'limited cultural background'; that Canada 'has had no serious problems with her native peoples') are recorded as claims of 1930, not adopted. The atlas has no communication-studies entry; the McLuhan introduction is noted from the catalogue only.

kenneth_pomeranz.label: Kenneth Pomeranz
kenneth_pomeranz.date_label: The Making of a Hinterland 1993 · The Great Divergence 2000 · exchange with Huang 2002–2003 · Journal of Global History 2006 · “Histories for a Less National Age” 2014
kenneth_pomeranz.description: A historian of China whose reciprocal comparisons of Eurasian core regions recast the divergence of European and Chinese economies. The Great Divergence (2000) takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as the reverse question and argues that 'Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path'. Coal, and land-intensive goods from New World colonies worked by enslaved people, relieved Europe's constraints of land and energy. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993), in its publisher’s description and Bianco’s review, traces the economic and ecological costs for inland North China when the late Qing and Republican state abandoned many hinterland areas. The Great Divergence became central to the debate over the “California School”. Philip Huang answered that England and the Yangzi delta stood “at opposite poles” of development and involution (2002–2003); Brenner and Isett located England’s divergence in early modern social-property relations (2002); Broadberry and Gupta found the advanced parts of Asia closer to Europe’s stagnating periphery in wages and prices (2006); Allen and colleagues disputed urban real-wage parity between the Yangzi delta and England (2011); and Broadberry, Guan and Li placed the divergence between leading regions around 1700 (2021). He was a co-founding editor of the Journal of Global History (2006), and his AHA presidential address (2014) asked how history might be reframed “for a less national age”.
kenneth_pomeranz.representative_figures_and_works: Kenneth Pomeranz (b. 1958); The Making of a Hinterland: State, Society, and Economy in Inland North China, 1853–1937 (1993); The Great Divergence: China, Europe, and the Making of the Modern World Economy (2000); “Beyond the East-West Binary” (2002) and “Facts are Stubborn Things” (2003), replies to Philip Huang; co-founding editor of the Journal of Global History (2006); “The Great Himalayan Watershed” (2009); “Histories for a Less National Age” (AHA presidential address, 2014). Readings: Bianco’s review (1996); Cooper’s review (2000); Huang (2002, 2003); Brenner and Isett (2002); Broadberry and Gupta (2006); Allen and colleagues (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li (2021).
kenneth_pomeranz.scope_note: This entry presents the argument of The Great Divergence as its introduction states it (pp. 3–27 read, with the contents, in a preview of the later Princeton edition; page numbers are that edition's). The Making of a Hinterland is checked at contents level and through Bianco's 1996 review, read in full; its text is unread. He is not presented as the originator of reciprocal comparison: he writes that the approach was 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong', takes the 'encompassing comparison' from Charles Tilly, and notes parallels with Sugihara Kaoru. Arguments from colonial extraction (Williams, Frank, Amin) precede his. His estimates are contested: Cooper (2000) notes 'plausible guesstimates', and Bianco (1996) judges that the 1993 book 'postule plus qu'il ne prouve' a deliberate strategy of selective development. Later critiques (Huang 2002–2003; Brenner and Isett 2002; Broadberry and Gupta 2006; Allen and colleagues 2011; Broadberry, Guan and Li 2021) appear as critique arrows and do not change what the 2000 introduction is read as arguing. The ‘California School’ is a label for Pomeranz, Wong and colleagues (AHA biography), not an atlas entry. The 2014 address is read through the AHA web text without pagination; the 2009 essay is dated from its opening only.

william_cronon.label: William Cronon
william_cronon.date_label: Changes in the Land 1983 · Nature’s Metropolis 1991 · “The Trouble with Wilderness” 1995
william_cronon.description: A historian of North American environments who treats ecological change as a two-way relation between people and the rest of nature, worked out through property, markets and ideas of nature. Changes in the Land (1983) assumes that 'the interactions of the two are dialectical' and finds in colonial New England not a choice between landscapes with and without people but 'two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'. Nature’s Metropolis (1991) follows grain, lumber and meat between Chicago and its hinterland on the premise that 'city and country have a common history, so their stories are best told together'. 'A Place for Stories' (1992) asks environmental historians for 'stories about stories about nature', and 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995) calls wilderness 'quite profoundly a human creation'. Reviewers found the Chicago book distant from farmers and townspeople, or moralising; he replied that he saw 'no pure heroes or pure villains'.
william_cronon.representative_figures_and_works: William Cronon (b. 1954); Changes in the Land: Indians, Colonists, and the Ecology of New England (1983); “Modes of Prophecy and Production: Placing Nature in History” (JAH 1990); Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991); “Kennecott Journey: The Paths out of Town” (1992); “A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative” (JAH 1992); “The Uses of Environmental History” (1993); “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995). Readings: the Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response (1992); Sessions’s reply on wilderness (1996); his own afterword to Changes in the Land (2003).
william_cronon.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-13: chapter 1 of Changes in the Land in an unpaginated web transcription; 'A Place for Stories' (JAH 1992; pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read) and 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993; OCR of the author’s scan, journal pagination); 'Kennecott Journey' (1992); passages of 'The Trouble with Wilderness' in the author’s reflow; and the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response read in full. Nature’s Metropolis itself is unread: its words appear here only as forum contributors quote them with page numbers. 'Modes of Prophecy and Production', his 1990 response to Worster in the JAH round table, is paywalled and unread. He is not presented as a founder. He places environmental history among the 'new' histories 'born or reenergized in the wake of the 1960s' (1993, p. 2), names Nash, Hays, Worster, Merchant, Tarr and Pyne as practitioners (pp. 2–3), footnotes lessons to Crosby, Richard White, McEvoy and others (pp. 8–10), and echoes Leopold (n. 11). On Mahoney’s reading (1992, p. 492), Nature’s Metropolis demonstrates 'this fundamental urban historical premise' rather than inventing it. His approaches were contested in period: Danbom (1992, p. 503) finds 'environmental moralism'; Mahoney (p. 491) that urban and economic history 'seem only to serve the interests of environmental history'; Sessions (1996) that the wilderness essay underweights wild habitat. His 2003 afterword, McNeill (2003) and Canadian uses after 2000 are later readings.

donald_worster.label: Donald Worster
donald_worster.date_label: Nature's Economy 1977 · Dust Bowl 1979 · Rivers of Empire 1985 · 'Transformations of the Earth' 1990
donald_worster.description: A historian of the American Great Plains and arid West who set out a three-level model of environmental history. In 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) he wrote that 'there are three levels on which the new history proceeds': 'understanding nature itself', 'the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment', and 'the purely mental or intellectual', which together 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. His 1990 Journal of American History essay turned to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena', chiefly the capitalist transformation of agriculture, which Dust Bowl (1979) had called 'the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature'; Rivers of Empire (1985) described the West as 'a modern hydraulic society'. Merchant's 1990 response called the levels 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field' but found that the essay 'lacks a gender analysis'. Cronon (1992) read Dust Bowl as a story whose 'chief agent' is capitalism and whose plot 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy'.
donald_worster.representative_figures_and_works: Donald Worster (b. 1941); Nature's Economy: The Roots of Ecology (1977); Dust Bowl: The Southern Plains in the 1930s (1979); Rivers of Empire: Water, Aridity, and the Growth of the American West (1985); 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', in The Ends of the Earth (1988); 'Transformations of the Earth: Toward an Agroecological Perspective in History', Journal of American History (1990), reprinted in The Wealth of Nature (1993). Readings: Merchant's round-table response (1990); Cronon, 'A Place for Stories' (1992); Hennessey's review of Rivers of Empire (1987); McDean (1986).
donald_worster.scope_note: This entry presents the three-level model in Worster's 1988 wording, checked in an abridged reprint and by full-text search of the 1988 edition, and the 1990 essay in his own 1993 reprint; the Journal of American History pages of 1990 were not reachable and are given only where another writer cites them (Isenberg 2013). Dust Bowl and Rivers of Empire are quoted at the pages given by Cronon (1992) and Hennessey (1987), with the wording confirmed by search of the original editions. He is not presented as the founder of the field or the sole author of the scheme: he grounds the idea in Aldo Leopold's call for 'an ecological interpretation of history', and Arthur McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. The scheme was contested at once: Merchant (1990) added gender and 'a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction', Cronon (1992) treated Dust Bowl as a declensionist narrative, and McDean (1986) criticised its generalisation across the Plains. The 1990 objections of White and Cronon in the round table are known here only through Isenberg (2013), a later reading.

alfred_crosby.label: Alfred W. Crosby
alfred_crosby.date_label: The Columbian Exchange 1972 · Virgin Soil Epidemics 1976 · Ecological Imperialism 1986
alfred_crosby.description: A historian of the biological consequences of European expansion. The Columbian Exchange (1972) followed pathogens, plants and animals between the Americas and the Old World after 1492, and 'Virgin Soil Epidemics' (1976) defined epidemics among peoples who, as Jones (2003, pp. 703–704) quotes the definition, 'have had no previous contact with the diseases that strike them' (the 1976 article itself is unread). Ecological Imperialism (1986) starts from the fact that 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation', asks why 'the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion', and suggests that 'the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component': crops, livestock, weeds and diseases helped Europeans make temperate 'Neo-Europes'. Later critics charge the model with ecological determinism and argue that the virgin-soil idea was flattened into a claim that Indigenous Americans had 'no immunity'.
alfred_crosby.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred W. Crosby (1931–2018); The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492 (1972); 'Virgin Soil Epidemics as a Factor in the Aboriginal Depopulation in America' (William and Mary Quarterly, 1976); Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986); 'The Past and Present of Environmental History' (American Historical Review, 1995). Readings: Miller's review (1987); Cook (1990); Cronon (1993); Subrahmanyam (1997); later, Jones (2003), McNeill (2003) and Isenberg (2013).
alfred_crosby.scope_note: This entry presents Ecological Imperialism as its prologue states the argument (pp. 1–7 read, with the contents and acknowledgments, in the publisher's sample of the 2004 second edition; page numbers are that edition's). The Columbian Exchange (1972), 'Virgin Soil Epidemics' (1976) and the 1995 AHR essay are unread: the 1972 book is characterised from Cook (1990) and McNeill (2003), and the 1976 wording is quoted as Jones (2003) quotes it. His 1978 American Heritage essay on New England, read in full, states the disease argument in his own words: 'Innocent of immunity or experience, the Indians were helpless.' He is not presented as the founder of environmental history: the ASEH's own history lists him among several 'founding members' with Worster, Flader and Opie, and in 1982 among 'the already widely known historians'; he thanks William McNeill, who 'read the whole thing in first draft'. Contested readings: in period, Subrahmanyam (1997) calls the books 'oft-cited (and oft-criticized)', while Miller (1987) finds Crosby 'careful not to overestimate the significance of any single component'. Later, McNeill (2003) records that 'Some readers felt that Crosby had relocated historical agency (and responsibility for genocide and colonialism) from humans to wheat and whooping cough'; Isenberg (2013) judges that his analysis 'devolved into little more than ecological determinism'; Jones (2003) argues that the virgin-soil model 'has been misunderstood and misrepresented', that the 1976 article itself stressed malnutrition and 'the social chaos generated by European colonization', and that Crosby's other writings stressed lack of immunity. These are later readings, not evidence for the edges. The 2004 preface, in which he calls Pomeranz's Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario', is a later self-reading and is not used.

carolyn_merchant.label: Carolyn Merchant
carolyn_merchant.date_label: The Death of Nature 1980 · Ecological Revolutions 1989 · Radical Ecology 1992
carolyn_merchant.description: A historian of science and environmental historian who argued in The Death of Nature (1980) that a science 'reconceptualizing reality as a machine rather than a living organism, sanctioned the domination of both nature and women'. In Ecological Revolutions (1989), a study of New England from 1600 to 1860, she treated major changes in human relations with nature as arising from tensions 'between a society’s mode of production and its ecology, and between its modes of production and reproduction', which in turn reshape consciousness. Answering Worster's three levels of ecology, production and cognition in 1990, she wrote that environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' and a gender analysis of each level. Her reading of Bacon's metaphors was disputed in the 1990s (Soble 1995; Pesic 1999, whom she answered in 2006), and a 1991 reviewer, praising her integration of gender, found 'painfully few people making history' in the New England book.
carolyn_merchant.representative_figures_and_works: Carolyn Merchant (b. 1936); The Death of Nature: Women, Ecology, and the Scientific Revolution (1980); “The Theoretical Structure of Ecological Revolutions” (1987); Ecological Revolutions: Nature, Gender, and Science in New England (1989); “Gender and Environmental History” (JAH round table, 1990); Radical Ecology: The Search for a Livable World (1992). Readings: Cronon (1993); Steinberg's review (1991); Soble (1995); Leach and Green (1997); Pesic (1999); Merchant's own retrospectives (1998, 2006).
carolyn_merchant.scope_note: This entry presents Merchant's framework as her own in-period texts state it: the 1987 Environmental Review article and the 1990 JAH response (both read in full, original pagination); The Death of Nature (1980) and Ecological Revolutions (1989) through author-hosted reprinted excerpts (pages are the reprints'); and the 1992 conclusion to Radical Ecology (facsimile, original pages). She is not presented as the founder of environmental history or of ecofeminism. She builds on Kuhn and on Marx and Engels, on Meillassoux, Peterson and Bridenthal for reproduction, and on Worster's levels; in 1998 she credits Hessen, Zilsel, Leiss and Kubrin ('It was Kubrin’s idea that the key concept of early modern science was that matter was dead'). She separates her socialist ecofeminism from a radical feminism that 'runs the risk of perpetuating the very value hierarchies it seeks to overthrow' (1989). The Bacon reading is contested (Soble 1995 and Pesic 1999, abstracts only), Leach and Green (1997) place The Death of Nature among the ecofeminist histories they criticise, and Steinberg (1991) faults the New England book's narrative. McNeill (2003) and Merchant's 2006 Isis response are later readings, not evidence for the 1980–1992 framework.

richard_white.label: Richard White
richard_white.date_label: Land Use, Environment, and Social Change 1980 · The Roots of Dependency 1983 · field survey 1985 · The Middle Ground 1991 · The Organic Machine 1995
richard_white.description: A historian of the American West, of Native American history and of environmental history. The Middle Ground (1991; quoted from Cambridge Core first-page excerpts of the introduction and chapters) rejects accounts of Indian–white contact with 'but two outcomes', conquest or persistence, because contact 'creates as well as destroys': in the Great Lakes pays d'en haut, French and Algonquian allies 'had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting', a middle ground which White describes as a process of creative and often expedient misunderstanding, sustained because whites could not simply command Indians or disregard them, until in the nineteenth century its compromises 'yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness'. His environmental books trace Salish and settler land use and environmental change in Island County, Washington (1980), subsistence, environment and dependency among the Choctaws, Pawnees and Navajos (1983), and the Columbia River as an organic machine, an energy system remade by human labour that keeps natural qualities, in which human work is energy as much as the river's flow (1995). His 1985 Pacific Historical Review essay surveyed environmental history as a new field, and he responded to Worster's agroecological essay in the 1990 Journal of American History round table.
richard_white.representative_figures_and_works: Richard White (b. 1947); Land Use, Environment, and Social Change: The Shaping of Island County, Washington (1980; 1992 paperback with Cronon's foreword and a new preface); The Roots of Dependency: Subsistence, Environment, and Social Change among the Choctaws, Pawnees, and Navajos (1983); “American Environmental History: The Development of a New Historical Field” (1985); “Environmental History, Ecology, and Meaning” (1990); The Middle Ground: Indians, Empires, and Republics in the Great Lakes Region, 1650–1815 (1991); The Organic Machine: The Remaking of the Columbia River (1995); “‘Are You an Environmentalist or Do You Work for a Living?’” (1995). Readings: Savard (1992), Edmunds (1993) and D. R. Miller (1994) on The Middle Ground; Cronon's foreword (1992) to Land Use.
richard_white.scope_note: Not Hayden White (node white). Witnesses for The Middle Ground: Cambridge Core first-page excerpts (full pages, folios observed) of the introduction (1991 p. ix) and of the chapters opening at pp. 50, 94 and 518; the next page of the introduction (1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi) and pp. 52–53 and 93 only in Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 twentieth-anniversary edition, whose body pagination matches 1991 at the pages checked (the equation 1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi is inferred from the introduction's opening at 1991 p. ix and 2011 p. xxv). The rest of the book is unread, and wording witnessed only by snippets is paraphrased in node text. Land Use (1980; 1992 paperback) and The Organic Machine (1995) are known from Google Books search-within snippets of their framing pages, not from page images; The Organic Machine's preface folios were not visible, so its framing is paraphrased. The Roots of Dependency (1983), the 1985 survey, the 1990 round-table response and the 1995 Uncommon Ground essay are unread (paywalled or not previewed) and are known through Cronon (1993, 1994), Worster (1990, Portuguese translation), Cook (1990), Isenberg (2013) and the publisher's records. He is not presented as a founder of environmental history: Land Use credits James Malin's neglected Great Plains studies as a trail to follow (snippet, p. 7), and Isenberg (2013) names him in a group of synthesisers. The middle ground was contested in period: Savard (1992) doubts its premise of Iroquois devastation, Edmunds (1993) finds the post-1770 chapters 'less convincing', and D. R. Miller (1994) notes the neglect of peoples neither Iroquoian nor Algonquian; Merrell's in-period critique (Into the American Woods, 1999) is known here only through White's later 2011 response. Havard (2003) and Deloria (2006) are later critiques, also known here only through that 2011 preface, a later reading. Canadian environmental historians cite him chiefly for the 1985 survey; Canadian use of The Middle Ground before 2000 is checked only in reviews and one legal article.

dipesh_chakrabarty.label: Dipesh Chakrabarty
dipesh_chakrabarty.date_label: Rethinking Working-Class History 1989 · “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History” 1992 · Provincializing Europe 2000 · “The Climate of History” 2009
dipesh_chakrabarty.description: A historian of modern South Asia in the Subaltern Studies collective. He argues that, within university-based historical discourse, an imagined 'Europe' remains its dominant theoretical reference: 'the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call “Indian,” “Chinese,” “Kenyan”', where 'Europe' and 'India' are 'hyperreal terms', figures of the imaginary 'subject to contestation' (1992). Rethinking Working-Class History (1989) reads Bengal’s jute-mill workers against an assumption of 'a hegemonic bourgeois culture' in Marx’s category of capital. 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (1992) calls Europe 'a silent referent in historical knowledge', and Provincializing Europe (2000) criticises the historicist 'first in Europe, then elsewhere' that placed colonized peoples in 'an imaginary waiting room of history', while holding European thought 'both indispensable and inadequate'; a 2000 essay separates History 1, the past 'posited by capital', from History 2, pasts that are 'not pasts separate from capital' but 'inhere in capital and yet interrupt and punctuate' its logic. In period, Sumit Sarkar called the trajectory he described 'debilitating', and the labour historian Rajnarayan Chandavarkar found a 'static, timeless, indeed Orientalist' culture in his Bengal book. After 2000, 'The Climate of History' (2009) argued that climate change spells 'the collapse of the age-old humanist distinction between natural history and human history'.
dipesh_chakrabarty.representative_figures_and_works: Dipesh Chakrabarty (b. 1948); Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (1989); “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History: Who Speaks for ‘Indian’ Pasts?” (Representations, 1992); “Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts” (Perspectives, 1997); Provincializing Europe: Postcolonial Thought and Historical Difference (2000); “Universalism and Belonging in the Logic of Capital” (Public Culture, 2000). After 2000: “The Climate of History: Four Theses” (Critical Inquiry, 2009). Readings: Nair’s review (1990); Dirlik (1994); Chandavarkar (1997); Sarkar (1997); Whose Anthropocene? (2016), with his response.
dipesh_chakrabarty.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the 1989 preface (pp. xi–xv) and introduction (pp. 3–6) in the publisher preview; 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (Representations 37, 1992, pp. 1–26) in full; the 1997 AHA essay in full (web text, no page numbers); the Provincializing Europe introduction (pp. 3–23, in the publisher’s excerpt); 'Universalism and Belonging in the Logic of Capital' (Public Culture, 2000), which he describes as a slightly different version of the book’s chapter 2; and 'The Climate of History' (2009) in full. The rest of the 1989 and 2000 books is unread, including chapter 2 itself. He is not presented as a founder. He calls Ranajit Guha 'the founder of the group' (1997) and writes that his 'argument for provincializing Europe follows directly from my involvement in this project' (2000, p. 15). The book’s critique of historicism builds on Guha’s rejection of Hobsbawm’s 'prepolitical' and cites Fabian’s 'denial of coevalness' (pp. 8, 11–15). Contested in period: by Sarkar (1997), by Chandavarkar (1997) and, in a critique aimed mainly at Prakash, by Dirlik (1994). O'Hanlon and Washbrook (1992) criticised the wider post-Orientalist programme, principally Prakash's, without naming him; only their opening page and notes were read. The 2009 essay and its reception (2014–16) are after 2000 and support only the separate environment edge, which is dated 2009 in its label and text; they are not evidence for any claim about his work before 2000.

bryan_d_palmer.label: Bryan D. Palmer
bryan_d_palmer.date_label: ‘Most Uncommon Common Men’ 1976 · A Culture in Conflict 1979 · ‘Response to Joan Scott’ 1987 · Descent into Discourse 1990 · E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions 1994 · ‘Radical Reasoning’ 2009
bryan_d_palmer.description: A Canadian historian of labour and the left who took up E. P. Thompson's account of class and culture and later defended historical materialism against the linguistic turn. His first essay in Labour/Le Travailleur (1976) traced artisan culture and restated what he called 'a standard axiom of an emerging social history': 'As a class for itself, the working class was born, not in the factory, but in the workshop'; the critic David Bercuson read his study of Hamilton's skilled workers (1979) as 'echoing E.P. Thompson' (1981). In the International Labor and Working-Class History forum of 1987 he answered Joan Scott's case for reconceiving labour history through language and gender, which on his reading reduced class and its material relations to discourse, while granting, as Ted McCoy (2021) quotes him, that 'to say that language matters is not to say it is all that matters'; and Descent into Discourse (1990) held, as the Marxist reviewer Alex Callinicos quoted it, that 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected', while granting that discourse theory 'contains insights and guides'. Scott replied that 'class struggle is produced in discourse', a discourse she took to include 'ways of organizing lives, institutions, societies', not words alone, and that there is no choice, 'as Bryan Palmer insists there is, between a focus on class or gender'; Callinicos, broadly sympathetic, suggested that his treatment of class might underestimate 'the objective determinants of subjective action' and noted that he took Thompson and Raymond Williams 'to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure'. In 2009 he criticised Ian McKay's liberal order as, in his reading, 'a seemingly trans-historical analytic framework' that 'sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism's changing historical structures'.
bryan_d_palmer.representative_figures_and_works: Bryan D. Palmer (b. 1951); “Most Uncommon Common Men: Craft and Culture in Historical Perspective” (Labour/Le Travailleur, 1976); A Culture in Conflict: Skilled Workers and Industrial Capitalism in Hamilton, Ontario, 1860–1914 (1979); The Making of E. P. Thompson: Marxism, Humanism, and History (1981); with Gregory S. Kealey, Dreaming of What Might Be: The Knights of Labor in Ontario, 1880–1900 (1982); Working-Class Experience (1983; 2nd ed. 1992); “Response to Joan Scott” (International Labor and Working-Class History, 1987); Descent into Discourse: The Reification of Language and the Writing of Social History (1990); “Homage to Edward Thompson” (Labour/Le Travail, 1993–94); E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions (1994). After 2000: Canada’s 1960s (2009); “Radical Reasoning” (Underhill Review, 2009). Readings: Bercuson (1981); Scott’s reply (1987); Callinicos (1992); Dissenting Traditions (2021), with essays by Rogers, McCoy and Pearson.
bryan_d_palmer.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: his 1976 Labour/Le Travailleur essay in full; the first page of his 1987 'Response to Joan Scott' (publisher's preview image) and its notes as listed by the publisher; Scott's 1987 essay (first page) and her 'A Reply to Criticism' (1987) in full; Bercuson (1981, pp. 95–97); Callinicos's 1992 review of Descent into Discourse in full; 'Homage to Edward Thompson' (1993–94), searched in full and read at pp. 67–68 (Part I) and 16–18 (Part II); and 'Radical Reasoning' (2009) in full. He is not presented as a founder: Freeman (2002) names him with Kealey and Sangster in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail, and the 1976 essay presents its thesis as 'a standard axiom of an emerging social history'. Contested in period by Bercuson (1981) on working-class culture, by Scott (1987) on language and gender, and, from a sympathetic Marxist position, by Callinicos (1992). The 2009 critique of the liberal order is dated in its label and text. The essays in Dissenting Traditions (2021) are later readings and are labelled as such wherever they are cited.

carl_berger.label: Carl Berger
carl_berger.date_label: The Sense of Power 1970 · The Writing of Canadian History 1976; 2nd ed. 1986
carl_berger.description: A University of Toronto historian of English-Canadian ideas. The Sense of Power (1970) is 'a study in Canadian nationalist thought': against the 'so-called liberal nationalist school', for which imperialism and nationalism added up to 'a struggle between the past and the future', he argued that 'Imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism', a 'type of awareness of nationality which rested upon a certain understanding of history, the national character, and the national mission'. The Writing of Canadian History (1976; second edition 1986) examines 'aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century' through the 'central teachings' of Wrong, Shortt, Martin, Innis, Lower, Underhill, Creighton and Morton, and treats written history as 'a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'; he left French-Canadian writing aside because the two language traditions had been 'preoccupied with the backgrounds of two rather different “nations”'. In period, Jacques Monet thought the imperialism thesis 'très difficile, sinon impossible, à réfuter' (1972), while Douglas Cole and Graham Carr held that it over-Canadianized a Britannic movement, Susan Mann Trofimenkoff called his imperialists' nationalism 'decidedly masculine' (1979), Allen Mills found that his account of all Canadian historians as nationalists put 'much too much weight on that over-used term' (1977), and Ronald Rudin rejected his assumption that historians were 'united by their search for the truth' (1997).
carl_berger.representative_figures_and_works: Carl Berger (b. 1939); ed., Imperialism and Nationalism, 1884–1914: A Conflict in Canadian Thought (1969); The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867–1914 (1970; 2nd ed. 2013, with an introduction by Doug Owram); The Writing of Canadian History: Aspects of English-Canadian Historical Writing, 1900–1970 (1976; 2nd ed., … since 1900, 1986, with a new chapter, 'Tradition and the “New” History'); Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983). Readings: Monet (1972); Mills (1977); Terry Cook (1977–78); Trofimenkoff (1979); Carr (1982); Karr (1989); Rudin (1997). Later reading: Owram (2013).
carl_berger.scope_note: This entry presents the two framework books. Neither could be read continuously: both are borrow-only on the Internet Archive. Berger's own words are quoted from Google Books snippet views (The Sense of Power, 2013 printing with the 1970 pagination: introduction pp. 3, 9–10, conclusion p. 259; The Writing of Canadian History, 1986 edition: both prefaces and pp. 181, 261–262, 289, 298, 312), and are corroborated by in-period reviews read in full: Monet (1972), Mills (1977) and Terry Cook (1977–78). Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983) is checked at metadata level only. He is not presented as the originator of the imperialism thesis: Monet notes that Norman Penlington's Canada and Imperialism (1965) had already suggested it. Contested in period: Page, Cole and Nelles (1970, as Monet reports them), Cole (1971), Carr (1982, journal abstract), Karr (1989) on the elite group-biography method, Trofimenkoff (1979) on women, and Rudin (1997) on French-Canadian writing and on the assumption of a common search for truth. No in-period text found here faults The Writing of Canadian History for treating only male historians; Trofimenkoff's critique is of the field. Owram's 2013 introduction is a later reading.

ramsay_cook.label: Ramsay Cook
ramsay_cook.date_label: “Canadian Centennial Cerebrations” 1967 · The Maple Leaf Forever 1971 · “Regionalism Unmasked” 1983 · The Regenerators 1985 · “Cabbages Not Kings” 1990 · “Identities Are Not Like Hats” 2000
ramsay_cook.description: An English-Canadian historian of nationalism, Quebec and Victorian thought. Attacking a nationalist manifesto in the centennial year, he suggested that 'instead of constantly deploring our lack of identity, we should attempt to understand and explain the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have. It might just be that it is in these limited identities that “Canadianism” is found' (1967, as quoted by Buckner); Careless made 'limited identities' a programme in 1969. Cook did not make region his unit of analysis: reviewing regional syntheses, he doubted 'the existence of the phenomena we have for so long called regions' and judged that 'as a tool of analysis, “regionalism” is a concept whose time has gone' (1983). The Regenerators (1985) read late Victorian social critics as replacing 'man's salvation' with 'a concern for social salvation', so that Christianity became 'less rather than more relevant' (as quoted by Gauvreau); Michael Gauvreau answered in 1991 that the book rests on 'military metaphors' that recent studies had abandoned, and a 1998 review named Cook, with David Marshall, the strongest advocate of the 'secularization thesis'. His lecture 'Cabbages Not Kings' (1990) proposed an ecological reading of contact in which 'Cabbages, at least as much as kings, led to the transformation of the new world'. In the quarrel over national history he called the debate between 'nationalists' and 'limited identitarians' 'arid' (1993), and in 2000 he argued that identities are 'contingent' and 'multiple rather than single'.
ramsay_cook.representative_figures_and_works: Ramsay Cook (1931–2016); Canada and the French-Canadian Question (1966); “Canadian Centennial Cerebrations” (International Journal, 1967); The Maple Leaf Forever: Essays on Nationalism and Politics in Canada (1971); Canada 1896–1921: A Nation Transformed (1974, with Robert Craig Brown); “The Burden of Regionalism” (Acadiensis, 1977); “Regionalism Unmasked” (Acadiensis, 1983); The Regenerators: Social Criticism in Late Victorian English Canada (1985); “Cabbages Not Kings: Towards an Ecological Interpretation of Early Canadian History” (Journal of Canadian Studies, 1990–91); “The New History of Atlantic Canada” (Acadiensis, 1993); “‘Identities Are Not Like Hats’” (Canadian Historical Review, 2000). Readings: Careless (1969); Gaffield (1986); Karr (1989); Gauvreau (1991); Marshall (1993–94); Buckner (2000).
ramsay_cook.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: three of Cook's Acadiensis review essays in full (1977, 1983, 1993), the opening of the 1967 article (OpenAlex text) and the abstract of his 2000 forum piece. The limited-identities sentence (1967) and the 1970 essay reprinted in The Maple Leaf Forever are known through Buckner's (2000) and Karr's (1989) quotations. The Regenerators is unread: its words appear here as quoted by Gauvreau (1991) and Karr, with Gaffield's 1986 review and the book's contents. 'Cabbages Not Kings' was read for the environment drafts on 2026-10-13 and is not re-read here. Canada and the French-Canadian Question is unread. He is not presented as a founder: Buckner says Cook coined 'limited identities' and Careless popularized it, and Cook wrote in 1995 that the phrase was 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (quoted by Buckner). Contested in period: Gauvreau (1991) on The Regenerators and on limited identities as a frame that marginalized religion; Karr (1989) on his 'anti-national crusade'; Buckner (2000) on the additive idea of identity he attributes to Cook and Careless. Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (1991–92) is read only in its abstract, which does not name Cook.

j_m_s_careless.label: J. M. S. Careless
j_m_s_careless.date_label: “Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History” 1954 · Brown of the Globe 1959–63 · “‘Limited Identities’ in Canada” 1969 · “Limited Identities — Ten Years Later” 1981 · Frontier and Metropolis 1989
j_m_s_careless.description: A University of Toronto historian of nineteenth-century Canada and biographer of George Brown (Brown of the Globe, 1959–63). 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History' (1954) criticised the Canadian historians who had adapted Turner's frontier thesis and proposed instead the study of the metropolis, a city that organizes a wide area 'through control of communications, trade, and finance'; in that view the frontier 'is in the largest sense a dependent', though 'if we reject a frontier determinism we should hardly replace it with a metropolitan determinism'. In 1969 he took up Ramsay Cook's phrase and argued that the Canadian experience must be understood through the 'limited identities of region, culture and class' (as quoted by Buckner, 2000); a decade later he added that 'Metropolitanism is not the antithesis of regionalism' and that limited identities 'should not limit his own perception' (1981). Frontier and Metropolis (1989), based on his 1987 Creighton Lectures, restated both themes. In period, Donald Davis (1985) judged his metropolitan approach 'of only limited usefulness in guiding research', and Phillip Buckner (2000) rejected the view, which he attributed to Careless and Granatstein, of regionalism as 'a construct designed to justify the dismantling of the Canadian state'.
j_m_s_careless.representative_figures_and_works: J. M. S. Careless (1919–2009); “Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History” (Canadian Historical Review, 1954); Brown of the Globe, vol. 1, The Voice of Upper Canada, 1818–1859 (1959) and vol. 2, Statesman of Confederation, 1860–1880 (1963); “‘Limited Identities’ in Canada” (Canadian Historical Review, 1969); “Limited Identities — Ten Years Later” (Manitoba History, 1981); Frontier and Metropolis: Regions, Cities, and Identities in Canada before 1914 (1989). Readings: Davis (1985); Szostak (1990); Irwin (1997); Buckner (2000).
j_m_s_careless.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the 1954 article in full (Canadian Historical Review 35:1, pp. 1–21, in an Internet Archive scan of the issue); the 1979 Jackson lecture 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' in full (Manitoba History no. 1, 1981, web text without page numbers); Davis (Urban History Review, 1985, pp. 95–113) in full; Szostak's review of Frontier and Metropolis (Journal of Economic History, 1990, pp. 499–501) in full; and Buckner (Acadiensis, 2000), pp. 4–10. The 1969 article is unread here: its wording is taken from Buckner's quotations and from Careless's own quotation of its last page in 1981. Frontier and Metropolis and Brown of the Globe are unread (catalogue records; the book's content through Szostak's review). He is not presented as the originator of either idea. In 1954 he credits metropolitanism to Lower, to Masters's Rise of Toronto (1947) and its source in N. S. B. Gras, and to the Laurentian school of Innis and Creighton (pp. 16–17); Davis (1985, p. 97) notes that Lower discussed metropolitanism 'some eight years before'. He wrote in 1981 that he 'did not invent the term “limited identity”' but acquired it from Ramsay Cook, so that his 1969 article 'was thus essentially a commentary on his initial idea'; Cook's coinage belongs to Cook's entry. Contested in period: by W. L. Morton and S. D. Clark (both as quoted by Davis), by Davis (1985), by Szostak (1990), by Irwin (1997, abstract) and by Buckner (2000). Michael Bliss (1991–92) is not recorded as a critic of Careless: Buckner (2000, p. 9) pairs Bliss's fragmentation charge with Careless's own later worry.

donald_creighton.label: Donald Creighton
donald_creighton.date_label: The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence 1937 · Dominion of the North 1944 · John A. Macdonald 1952, 1955 · CHA presidential address 1957 · “The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence” 1969 · Canada’s First Century 1970
donald_creighton.description: A Toronto historian whose The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) built Canadian history around the one river system 'that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent', which inspired Canadians 'to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior' (his own restatement of 1969); Dominion of the North (1944) calls the river 'the natural basis of a great commercial empire' and beaver fur 'the first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system'. His two-volume John A. Macdonald (1952, 1955) completed what he called 'a trilogy on one theme'; in 1969 he accepted 'the parentage of an idea' others called 'the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history', but rejected the story that his first book was 'the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis'. As president of the Canadian Historical Association (1957) he attacked the Liberal 'Authorized Version' of Canadian history and the imported 'Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'Frontier thesis', and in 1969 he traced the 'decline and fall' of the Empire of the St. Lawrence and of the Canada built on it, calling official bilingualism and a special position for Quebec 'a repudiation of the intentions of the Fathers of Confederation'. Contested in period: Michel Brunet (1953) found the Macdonald biography full of 'nombreux préjugés', Guy Frégault (1955) asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ?', and W. L. Morton, as Davis (1985) reports him, held that the metropolitan view he associated with Creighton seemed 'necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland'. From the late 1960s the national frame the Laurentian narrative supported gave way to regional history and 'limited identities' (Buckner, 2000).
donald_creighton.representative_figures_and_works: Donald Creighton (1902–1979); The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence, 1760–1850 (1937; reissued as The Empire of the St. Lawrence, 1956); Dominion of the North: A History of Canada (1944); John A. Macdonald: The Young Politician (1952) and The Old Chieftain (1955); Presidential Address, Canadian Historical Association (1957); Harold Adams Innis: Portrait of a Scholar (1957); “The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence” (1969); Canada’s First Century, 1867–1967 (1970). Readings: Heaton (1938); Brunet (1953); Frégault (1955); Woodcock (1979); Ouellet (1984); Davis (1985); Salmon (1997); Buckner (2000).
donald_creighton.scope_note: This entry presents the Laurentian narrative and Creighton's later nationalism. Read on 2026-10-14: his 1957 presidential address (pp. 1–12) and his 1969 lecture 'The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence' (pp. 14–25), both in full from page images; Dominion of the North (1944) at its contents and selected pages (pp. 21, 24–25, 166, 270, 272, 298, 419, 505–507) in an open Internet Archive copy. The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) itself is unread: the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only, and its argument is checked through the 1944 book, his own 1969 retrospect (labelled as such) and the first page of Herbert Heaton's 1938 review. He is not presented as the founder of a school: in 1969 he reported that others regarded the 1937 phrase as 'the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school' and the 'genesis' of 'the Laurentian interpretation', and said only that he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea'. The Innis lineage is recorded as contested: readers from Woodcock (1979) and Ouellet (1984) to Salmon (1997) tie the book to Innis's staple studies, while Creighton said the subject was suggested by W. P. M. Kennedy, 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time'. The 1957 and 1969 texts are polemics; their judgements of Mackenzie King, Quebec and bilingualism are recorded as his claims, not adopted. Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) and his later hinterland critique are known here only through Davis (1985); Careless's 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism' (1954), Berger's chapter on Creighton (1976), Canada's First Century (1970) and the Innis biography (1957) are unread (catalogue or review level only).

joy_parr.label: Joy Parr
joy_parr.date_label: Labouring Children 1980 · 'Nature and Hierarchy' 1985 · The Gender of Breadwinners 1990 · 'Gender History and Historical Practice' 1995 · Domestic Goods 1999 · Sensing Changes 2010
joy_parr.description: A Canadian historian of work, gender, childhood, consumption and the environment. In 1985 she wrote that what set women and children apart as historical subjects was not nature but 'proximity to power', and asked historians to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict'. The Gender of Breadwinners (1990) tested this in two Ontario towns, Paris, a knitting-mill town where most wage earners were women, and Hanover, a furniture town where most were men; reviewers quote it rejecting 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' and treating 'class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' as pairs whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. In the Left History exchange of 1995–96 Iacovetta and Kealey called her 'a major figure in the field' of gender history, while Sangster criticised the tie her 1995 essay drew between gender history and 'the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships'; the labour historian Craig Heron praised the book but found that it had 'suppressed the impact of class' in a 1949 strike. Labouring Children (1980) grew from her Yale thesis on British child immigrants; later books turned to postwar household goods (Domestic Goods, 1999) and to sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change (Sensing Changes, 2010).
joy_parr.representative_figures_and_works: Joy Parr (1949–2024); PhD Yale 1977 ('The Home Children: British Juvenile Immigrants to Canada, 1868–1924'); Labouring Children: British Immigrant Apprentices to Canada, 1869–1924 (1980); Childhood and Family in Canadian History (ed., 1982); “Nature and Hierarchy: Reflections on Writing the History of Women and Children” (Atlantis, 1985); “Disaggregating the Sexual Division of Labour” (CSSH, 1988); The Gender of Breadwinners: Women, Men, and Change in Two Industrial Towns, 1880–1950 (1990); “Gender History and Historical Practice” (CHR, 1995; reprinted in Gender and History in Canada, ed. with Mark Rosenfeld, 1996); “Household Choices as Politics and Pleasure in 1950s Canada” (ILWCH, 1999); Domestic Goods: The Material, the Moral, and the Economic in the Postwar Years (1999). After 2000: “Smells Like?” (Environmental History, 2006); Sensing Changes: Technologies, Environments, and the Everyday, 1953–2003 (2010). Readings: Drystek (1980); Heron, Guildford, Scheinberg and Dennis (1991); Bertaux (1992); Benson (1993); the Left History exchange (Sangster 1995, 1996; Dubinsky and Marks 1996; Iacovetta and Kealey 1996); Brush (2000); Owram (2001); Jackson and Rumiel (2011).
joy_parr.scope_note: Her own words are read in 'Nature and Hierarchy' (Atlantis, 1985, pp. 39–44, in full), the first-page extract of the 1988 CSSH article and the abstract of the 1999 ILWCH article. Her books are not read here: The Gender of Breadwinners, Domestic Goods and Sensing Changes are quoted only as their reviewers quote them, with the reviewers' page references, and the 1995 CHR essay only as Iacovetta and Kealey (1996) and Sangster (1996) quote it. In-period reviews read in full: Drystek (1980), Heron (CHR, 1991), Guildford (Atlantis, 1991), Scheinberg (Archivaria, 1991), Dennis (EcHR, 1991), Bertaux (JEH, 1992), Benson (JAH, 1993), Brush (EH.NET, 2000); later reception: Owram (BC Studies, 2001); the four Left History papers of 1995–96 are read in full. She is not presented as a founder: her 1985 essay places itself among 'a good many others' asking for the change, and the Canadian gender-history debate also turned on Pierson (1991) and Scott. The 1995 CHR essay appeared in an issue of historiographical essays, not in a CHR exchange; the exchange that took it up was in Left History. The environmental work dates from 2006–10 and is used only for the environment edge; a 2026 CHR forum on The Gender of Breadwinners is a later reading.

mariana_valverde.label: Mariana Valverde
mariana_valverde.date_label: “The Struggles of the Immoral” (with Weir) 1988 · The Age of Light, Soap, and Water 1991 · “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State” 1992 · Diseases of the Will 1998 · Law’s Dream of a Common Knowledge 2003
mariana_valverde.description: A sociologist and criminologist, not a historian by training (PhD in social and political thought, York, 1982; University of Toronto Centre of Criminology from 1993); historians read her study of social purity in English Canada as a statement of moral regulation. The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) follows reformers who sought 'to reshape the ethical subjectivity of both immigrants and native-born Canadians' and argues that their movements 'helped to shape the bourgeoisie, which led the movements, as well as the working class'; her notes trace the term to Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch but 'restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity', and she held, as 'Foucault and his followers have pointed out', that 'the state has no monopoly on moral regulation'. In 1992 she endorsed Mitchell Dean's argument that classical liberalism was 'a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation' and faulted Jean-Marie Fecteau's account of relief institutions as means of class control as 'a rather functionalist formulation'. Historians used and contested the frame: Tina Loo asked that it 'address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance' (1992), Donald Wright found that the reformers' silent audiences gave 'the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (1995), and Nancy Christie and Michael Gauvreau wrote that she and Doug Owram 'have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from “progressive” currents of modern thought and social action' (1996). Later books turn to alcohol and the will (Diseases of the Will, 1998) and to law (Law's Dream of a Common Knowledge, 2003).
mariana_valverde.representative_figures_and_works: Mariana Valverde (b. 1955); “The Struggles of the Immoral: Preliminary Remarks on Moral Regulation” (with Lorna Weir, Resources for Feminist Research, 1988); “Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?” (Labour/Le Travail, 1990); The Age of Light, Soap, and Water: Moral Reform in English Canada, 1885–1925 (1991; reissued 2008 with a new introduction); “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State” (Labour/Le Travail, 1992); Gender Conflicts (ed. with Franca Iacovetta, 1992); Studies in Moral Regulation (ed., 1994); “Deconstructive Marxism” (Labour/Le Travail, 1995); Diseases of the Will: Alcohol and the Dilemmas of Freedom (1998). After 2000: Law’s Dream of a Common Knowledge (2003); “Introduction to the 2008 Edition” of The Age of Light, Soap, and Water. In-period readings: Loo, Dehli and McCormick (reviews, 1992); Wright (1995); Christie and Gauvreau (1996); Strange and Loo, Making Good (1997); Hunt (1997, 1999).
mariana_valverde.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-14: her review essays 'Poststructuralist Gender Historians' (1990) and 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State' (1992) in full, and 'Deconstructive Marxism' (1995) at pp. 329–332; four in-period reviews or review essays of The Age of Light, Soap, and Water in full (Loo 1992, Dehli 1992, McCormick 1992) or in their Valverde section (Wright 1995, pp. 122–126). The book itself is known here only through those reviewers' quotations and through search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, which keeps the 1991 pagination for the original text (checked: pp. 15, 17, 165 and 166 match the 1992 reviewers' page references; the 1991 preface's p. 9 appears as p. ix). Christie and Gauvreau (1996), Strange and Loo (1997), Hunt (1999) and Diseases of the Will (1998) are known only through such snippets. 'The Struggles of the Immoral' (1988, with Lorna Weir) is unread. She is not presented as the originator of moral regulation: Corrigan (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer (1985) precede her, and she credits their theorization as 'influential here' while finding that it obscures 'the agencies of regulation internal to civil society'. She called herself a sociologist working between disciplines; Loo (1992) and Wright (1995) read her that way, and the 2008 introduction, a later reading, says that 'no history department in Canada would ever hire me'. The 2003 book is cited at title level only; the 2008 introduction is a later reading and carries no claim about the 1990s.
