ranajit_guha.label: Ranajit Guha
ranajit_guha.date_label: A Rule of Property for Bengal 1963 · “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India” 1982 · Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency 1983 · “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency” 1983 · “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography” 1989 (book 1997)
ranajit_guha.description: A historian of colonial India, who taught at Sussex and the Australian National University and edited Subaltern Studies from its first volume (1982) until he left the editorial team in 1988. The opening statement holds that the historiography of Indian nationalism 'has for a long time been dominated by elitism—colonialist elitism and bourgeois-nationalist elitism', and that it leaves out 'the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain' that 'neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', while allowing 'a great deal of overlap' between the two (1982). Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983) attributes 'a consciousness' to the rebel peasant, holds that Hobsbawm's 'pre-political' 'helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India', and reads that consciousness through the records of counter-insurgency; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (1983) finds colonial, nationalist and radical histories alike making the rebel 'only a contingent element in another history with another subject'. 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (1989; book 1997) defines hegemony, against 'the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony', as dominance in which 'Persuasion (P) outweighs Coercion (C)', and argues that colonial dominance had 'quite erroneously been endowed with hegemony'. In period, Spivak (1985) read the recovery of subaltern consciousness as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', O'Hanlon (1988) found 'the classic figure of Western humanism' readmitted 'in the figure of the subaltern himself', Bayly (1988) found that the approach sometimes seemed to postulate an 'unchanging peasantry', and Sarkar (1997) an 'unnoticed drift' towards nationalist positions 'even in Guha's initial formulation of the project'.
ranajit_guha.representative_figures_and_works: Ranajit Guha (1923–2023); A Rule of Property for Bengal: An Essay on the Idea of Permanent Settlement (Paris: Mouton, 1963); Preface and “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India”, Subaltern Studies I (1982); Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (Delhi, 1983); “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency”, Subaltern Studies II (1983); “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography”, Subaltern Studies VI (1989), and Dominance without Hegemony: History and Power in Colonial India (1997); Selected Subaltern Studies, edited with Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (1988). Readings: Spivak (1985); O'Hanlon (1988); Bayly (1988); Sarkar (1997); Chakrabarty (2000).
ranajit_guha.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the Subaltern Studies I preface and opening statement in the Selected Subaltern Studies reprint (1988, pp. 35–44); the introduction of Elementary Aspects (pp. 1–17), its bibliography and pp. 89–90; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (Subaltern Studies II, 1983, pp. 1–42) in full; and 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (Subaltern Studies VI, 1989), pp. 210–215, 227–233, 276–277, 291–292 and 299–303. The 1963 and 1997 books are known here only from metadata and from later quotation; the rest of Elementary Aspects and of the 1989 essay is unread. He is not presented as the founder of a field. In period, Chakrabarty called him 'the founder of the group' (1997) and James C. Scott wrote that Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document' of 'the Subaltern Studies School', while finding 'school' too rigid a term (1999); his own 1982 statement claims 'no more than to try and indicate an orientation'. Contested in period by Spivak (1985, a reading from within the project), O'Hanlon (1988), Bayly (1988) and Sarkar (1997); Javeed Alam's Marxist critique (Social Scientist, 1983) is known only through O'Hanlon and is unread. Vinay Bahl (1997) is unread. Chakrabarty's 2000 account of the project is a member's later reading and carries no edge alone. Not Ramachandra Guha, the environmental historian, who has a separate people record.

fernand_ouellet.label: Fernand Ouellet
fernand_ouellet.date_label: “La crise agricole dans le Bas-Canada” (with Jean Hamelin) 1962 · Histoire économique et sociale du Québec, 1760–1850 1966 · Éléments d’histoire sociale du Bas-Canada 1972 · Le Bas-Canada, 1791–1840 1976 (English adaptation 1980) · “Le mythe de « l’habitant sensible au marché »” 1976 · “La modernisation de l’historiographie” 1985
fernand_ouellet.description: A Laval historian whose economic and social history of Quebec, in a conjunctural idiom whose debt to Labrousse and Chaunu he acknowledged (as Savard reports), made an agricultural crisis the hinge of Lower Canadian history: with Jean Hamelin he argued in 1962 that after 1802 'la tendance majeure se renverse' and that 'la révolution de 1837-38 apparaît-elle, en grande partie, comme une réponse détournée aux problèmes posés par l'action conjointe des tensions démographiques et de la crise agricole', while adding that the crisis was not 'le seul moteur' of those years. The explanation joined prices and population to mentalities: the crisis revealed 'deux entités culturelles' with 'une grande disparité dans leur degré d'évolution' (1962), and in 1976 he held that the habitant who had adapted to the export market before 1802 then 'se durcit et résiste aux pressions en faveur de la rénovation du système agricole'. Contested in period: Gilles Paquet and Jean-Pierre Wallot (1972) found that, 'comme la plupart de ses prédécesseurs', he painted the habitants as 'désespérément embourbés dans des traditions routinières', and judged the thesis 'irrecevable'; Pierre Tousignant (1980) wrote that the Ouellet of the 1966 book 'faisait écho aux vieux préjugés de l'historiographie canadienne-anglaise', and that in the 1976 synthesis, where the 'retard des mentalités' no longer stood 'au premier plan', there was 'une notable amélioration'; Allan Greer (1981) answered that blaming the habitants for their predicament 'would be adding ideological insult to economic injury'. In 1985 he surveyed the turn of Quebec historiography to social history, reading the Montreal school's Conquest thesis, Séguin's 'décapitation' of the national élite, and its later softening as nationalist schemes.
fernand_ouellet.representative_figures_and_works: Fernand Ouellet (1926–2021); with Jean Hamelin, “La crise agricole dans le Bas-Canada, 1802–1837” (1962); Histoire économique et sociale du Québec, 1760–1850: structures et conjoncture (1966, preface by Robert Mandrou); Éléments d’histoire sociale du Bas-Canada (1972); Le Bas-Canada, 1791–1840: changements structuraux et crise (1976; English adaptation Lower Canada, 1791–1840: Social Change and Nationalism, 1980); “Le mythe de « l’habitant sensible au marché »” (1976); “La modernisation de l’historiographie et l’émergence de l’histoire sociale” (1985). Critics and readers: Paquet and Wallot (1972); Le Goff (1974); Tousignant (1980); Greer (1981, 1993); Dessureault (1998); Cardinal (1999); Savard (1974); Bouchard (1990); Rudin (1995).
fernand_ouellet.scope_note: This entry presents the agricultural-crisis and mentalities explanation of Lower Canada and Ouellet's later account of Quebec historiography. Read on 2026-10-14: the 1962 article with Hamelin (pp. 17–33), his 1976 reply to his critics (pp. 115–132) and his 1985 survey (pp. 11–29, 38, 47, 51–52, 64–68), all in full or in the parts named, from Érudit page images. His books (1966, 1972, 1976) are unread; their words appear only as Paquet and Wallot (1972) and Tousignant (1980) quote them, labelled so. He is not presented as the founder of social history in Quebec: Bouchard (1990, ¶13) says Ouellet and Hamelin 'avec quelques autres, ont introduit ici l'histoire sociale'. Le Goff's review of the controversy (1974) and Paquet and Wallot's CHR reply (1975) are unread; Ouellet reports that Le Goff concluded for a crisis 'dès le début du XIXe siècle'. Greer's Patriots and the People (1993) is unread; its relation to Ouellet is given in reviewers' words (Dessureault 1998, Cardinal 1999), not as Greer's. Ouellet's 1995 review essay on Greer (Histoire sociale) could not be reached. Judgements on French Canadians, the Patriotes and nationalism quoted here are his claims, not adopted.

gregory_s_kealey.label: Gregory S. Kealey
gregory_s_kealey.date_label: ‘The Honest Workingman’ 1976 · ‘The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing’ 1978 · Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism 1980 · ‘Prospects in the 1980s’ 1981 · Dreaming of What Might Be (with Palmer) 1982 · ‘1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt’ 1984 · Class, Gender, and Region 1988 · RCMP Security Bulletins (with Whitaker) 1989–97 · Spying on Canadians 2017
gregory_s_kealey.description: A Canadian historian of the working class, and later of political policing, who argued for putting class at the centre of Canadian history. Of Toronto's craftsmen he wrote that 'Skilled workers in the nineteenth century exercised far more power than we have previously realized', amounting to 'a high degree of workers' control of production' (1976); in 1981 he held that 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history', and he criticised the regional turn, under which 'Canadian historians have come to believe everything was different everywhere', as he had criticised the 'so-called "limited identities"' in 1978. David Brody, reviewing Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism (1980), found it marked by 'what might be termed the Gutman school' and a useful foundation, but judged that Kealey had 'overreached himself' in its interpretation; Bettina Bradbury (1987) faulted him and Bryan Palmer for partially dismissing a Knights of Labor editor's picture of the ideal working-class wife as 'crude moralizing', and Joan Sangster (2000) found in both men's early books 'a proclivity to centre on skilled male workers and their actions in the public sphere'. From the late 1980s he edited the RCMP's security bulletins with Reg Whitaker and studied state surveillance of labour and the left, concluding that 'For the RCMP the Cold War began in 1919, not in 1946' (1992).
gregory_s_kealey.representative_figures_and_works: Gregory S. Kealey (b. 1948); with Russell Hann, Linda Kealey and Peter Warrian, Primary Sources in Canadian Working Class History, 1860–1930 (1973); “‘The Honest Workingman’ and Workers’ Control: The Experience of Toronto Skilled Workers, 1860–1892” (Labour/Le Travailleur, 1976); with Peter Warrian, eds., Essays in Canadian Working Class History (1976); “The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing” (Acadiensis, 1978); Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism, 1867–1892 (1980); “Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s” (Labour/Le Travailleur, 1981); with Bryan D. Palmer, Dreaming of What Might Be: The Knights of Labor in Ontario, 1880–1900 (1982); “1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt” (Labour/Le Travail, 1984); “The Structure of Canadian Working-Class History” (1985); ed., Class, Gender, and Region: Essays in Canadian Historical Sociology (1988); with Reg Whitaker, eds., R.C.M.P. gregory_s_kealey.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14, all in the journals' own PDFs unless stated: his 1976 Labour/Le Travailleur essay (pp. 32–34 and 58–62 read closely, the rest skimmed); his 1978 Acadiensis review essay (pp. 116–117 and 134–135, UNB Libraries PDF); his 1981 'Prospects in the 1980s' in full; '1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt' (1984), pp. 11–17 and 34 and the conclusion; his introduction to Class, Gender, and Region (1988), pp. 1–7, in the CCLH reprint on AU Press's site; and the opening of his 1992 RCMP documentary article (pp. 169–171). sylvia_van_kirk.label: Sylvia Van Kirk
sylvia_van_kirk.date_label: “Many Tender Ties” 1980 · “The Reputation of a Lady” 1986 · “Tracing the Fortunes of Five Founding Families of Victoria” 1997–98 · “From ‘Marrying-In’ to ‘Marrying-Out’” 2002
sylvia_van_kirk.description: A Canadian historian of women in fur-trade society and of families of mixed descent in colonial Red River and Victoria. 'Many Tender Ties' (1980) treated traders' marriages with Indigenous and later mixed-descent women, à la façon du pays, as the core of a fur-trade society; as a 1981 reviewer quoted it, the book set out to show that the trade 'constituted a social and cultural complex as well as an economic activity' and claimed support for 'the claims of theorists in women's history that sex roles should constitute a category of historical investigation'. Her later articles turn on race and gender: the missionaries' 'racist attitudes, particularly with regard to women' and the rivalry among women 'compounded by the issue of race' in Red River (1986), and an acculturation in early Victoria that was 'gendered' (1997–98). Reviewers paired the book with Jennifer Brown's Strangers in Blood from 1981. One found its picture of fur-trade unions 'may be too complimentary', and Emma LaRocque (1999) placed her with Brown, Trigger and others in a 'neo cross-cultural approach' which, 'Compared to earlier racist material', was 'a much improved approach to Native history', but whose ethnological description 'results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable'.
sylvia_van_kirk.representative_figures_and_works: Sylvia Van Kirk; PhD, University of London, 1975, on women in fur-trade society, supervised by Glyndwr Williams (per Brown 2012; thesis unread); “Many Tender Ties”: Women in Fur-Trade Society in Western Canada, 1670–1870 (Winnipeg: Watson & Dwyer, 1980; Norman: University of Oklahoma Press, 1983); “What if Mama Is an Indian?: The Cultural Ambivalence of the Alexander Ross Family” (in Peterson and Brown, eds., The New Peoples, 1985; title only); “The Reputation of a Lady: Sarah Ballenden and the Foss-Pelly Scandal” (Manitoba History, 1986); two papers on the trader George Nelson (1984, 1988; titles only, per Brown 2012); “Tracing the Fortunes of Five Founding Families of Victoria” (BC Studies, 1997–98). After 2000: “From ‘Marrying-In’ to ‘Marrying-Out’: Changing Patterns of Aboriginal/Non-Aboriginal Marriage in Colonial Canada” (Frontiers, 2002); Brownlie and Korinek, eds., Finding a Way to the Heart (2012), essays in her honour. Readings: Bowsfield (1981); Gagan and Turner (1982); Brown (1983); Pierson (1992, reference list only); LaRocque (1999); McPherson (2000); Fiske (2000). Later readings: Perry (2008); Brown (2012).
sylvia_van_kirk.scope_note: Her own words are read in 'The Reputation of a Lady' (Manitoba History 11, 1986; the society's web edition, read in full, without page numbers) and in 'Tracing the Fortunes of Five Founding Families of Victoria' (BC Studies 115/116, 1997–98, pp. 149–51 only: the journal PDF is damaged after its seventh page). 'Many Tender Ties' is not read: Internet Archive copies are borrow-only and search-inside returned 'Item not available', and the Google Books quota was exhausted. The book is quoted only as Bowsfield (1981) quotes it, without page references, and as LaRocque (1999) cites pp. 101–103. Her 1977 CHA paper 'Women in Between' sits on Érudit and was not fetched. In-period readings read in full: Bowsfield (Archivaria 12, 1981), Gagan and Turner (Archivaria 14, 1982), Brown (CJNS, 1983), LaRocque (dissertation, 1999, PDF pp. 54 and 249), McPherson and Fiske (Atlantis 25:1, 2000). Later readings, labelled as such: Perry (Left History, 2008) and Brown (2012, read in its 2017 reprint). She is not presented as a founder: Bowsfield reviews her book within a fur-trade literature already being recast by Ray, Trigger and others, and Perry (2008, n. 4) notes that she and Brown 'were not entirely alone in this', naming Dickason, Peterson, Foster and Spry. The early-1990s critiques that Perry names (Pierson 1992; Emberley 1990–91) are not read; Project MUSE returned a verification page. No identity classification is recorded for any critic named here.

jennifer_s_h_brown.label: Jennifer S. H. Brown
jennifer_s_h_brown.date_label: Strangers in Blood 1980 · “Woman as Centre and Symbol in the Emergence of Metis Communities” 1983 · The New Peoples (ed. with Peterson) 1985 · The Orders of the Dreamed (with Brightman) 1988 · “Ethnohistorians: Strange Bedfellows, Kindred Spirits” 1991 · Reading Beyond Words (ed. with Vibert) 1996 · An Ethnohistorian in Rupert’s Land 2017
jennifer_s_h_brown.description: An anthropologist and historian of fur-trade families, the Métis, and Cree and Ojibwe history in the old Hudson's Bay Company territory. Strangers in Blood (1980) compared Hudson's Bay Company officers and North West Company partners as husbands and fathers; as a 1981 reviewer quoted it, the title took the British legal term for any relationship 'that the law refused to admit as legitimate' as 'one way of characterizing the meetings of Whites and Indians' in the fur trade. In 1983 she asked how women shaped Métis emergence, finding among North West Company fathers who had children baptized in Montreal that daughters were twice as likely as sons to stay in the Indian country, and in 1985 she co-edited with Jacqueline Peterson The New Peoples: Being and Becoming Métis in North America. As president of the American Society for Ethnohistory she spoke of 'our field, methodology, approach, or whatever it is we do when we do ethnohistory' (1991). A 1981 reviewer found the book weighed down by 'bits of anthropological theory'; Emma LaRocque (1999) placed her with Van Kirk in a 'neo cross-cultural approach', 'a much improved approach' on earlier work that still othered its subjects; and later scholarship rejects defining Métis by mixed descent, the biological starting point ('the meeting and mingling of Indian and white racial groups') that her 1983 essay set against a complex social history.
jennifer_s_h_brown.representative_figures_and_works: Jennifer S. H. Brown (b. 1940); doctoral study in anthropology at the University of Chicago, the dissertation revised as Strangers in Blood (per Brown 2012, 2017; dissertation unread); “A Demographic Transition in the Fur Trade Country” and “Changing Views of Fur Trade Marriage and Domesticity” (Western Canadian Journal of Anthropology, 1976); “Linguistic Solitudes and Changing Social Categories” (in Judd and Ray, eds., Old Trails and New Directions, 1980); Strangers in Blood: Fur Trade Company Families in Indian Country (Vancouver: UBC Press, 1980); “Children of the Early Fur Trades” (in Parr, ed., Childhood and Family in Canadian History, 1982); “Woman as Centre and Symbol in the Emergence of Metis Communities” (Canadian Journal of Native Studies, 1983); The New Peoples (ed. with Jacqueline Peterson, 1985), including her “Diverging Identities: The Presbyterian Métis of St. Gabriel Street, Montreal”; The Orders of the Dreamed: George Nelson on Cree and Northern Ojibwa Religion and Myth, 1823 (with Robert Brightman, 1988); “The Blind Men and the Elephant: Fur Trade History Revisited” (1990); “Ethnohistorians: Strange Bedfellows, Kindred Spirits” (Ethnohistory, 1991); Reading Beyond Words: Contexts for Native History (ed. with Elizabeth Vibert, 1996). After 2000: “Partial Truths: A Closer Look at Fur Trade Marriage” (2001); “‘All These Stories About Women’: ‘Many Tender Ties’ and a New Fur Trade History” (2012); An Ethnohistorian in Rupert’s Land: Unfinished Conversations (2017). Readings: Gresko (1981); Bowsfield (1981); Gagan and Turner (1982); LaRocque (1999); Fiske (2000); McPherson (2000). Later readings: Perry (2008); Gaudry (2013).
jennifer_s_h_brown.scope_note: Her own in-period words are read in 'Woman as Centre and Symbol in the Emergence of Metis Communities' (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, 1983, pp. 39–46, in full) and in an indexed excerpt only of her 1991 presidential address (Ethnohistory 38:2; OpenAlex's abstract field; p. 113 is the recorded first page, and the page itself was not inspected). Strangers in Blood and The New Peoples are not read: the Internet Archive copy of the 1980 book is borrow-only, and the 1985 collection is title-level. The book is quoted only as Gresko (1981) quotes it. An Ethnohistorian in Rupert's Land (2017, open access) was read in part: its acknowledgements, part introductions, chapter 3 and the opening of chapter 9 (reprints of 1990 and 1985 essays), and chapter 11 (her 2012 essay on Van Kirk). The 2017 reprints are labelled as later texts. The press notes that some chapter titles were modified, and chapter 3 cites a 2014 book, so the reprints do not witness the 1985 or 1990 wording. In-period readings read in full: Gresko (Canadian Woman Studies, 1981), Bowsfield (Archivaria, 1981), Gagan and Turner (Archivaria, 1982), LaRocque (1999, PDF p. 249), Fiske and McPherson (Atlantis, 2000). Later readings: Perry (2008), Gaudry (2013). She is not presented as a founder of Métis or fur-trade social history: her 1983 essay sets her questions beside Peterson's and Van Kirk's, and The New Peoples came from a 1981 Newberry Library conference that she helped organise. sherry_olson.label: Sherry Olson
sherry_olson.date_label: 'Baltimore Imitates the Spider' 1979 · Baltimore: The Building of an American City 1980 · 'Occupations and Residential Spaces' 1989 · 'Le peuplement de Montréal' 1997 · MAP, Montréal, l'avenir du passé, from 2000 · Peopling the North American City (with Patricia Thornton) 2011 · 'Rebuilding a Neighbourhood of Montreal' (with Dufaux) 2014
sherry_olson.description: A historical geographer, at Johns Hopkins and then McGill, whose Baltimore: The Building of an American City (1980) is 'about city building', read as 'a boom-and-bust sequence of "long swings," with eighteen years or so separating the neighboring peaks'. In Montreal she and her collaborators, among them the demographer Patricia Thornton, followed sampled families through parish registers, censuses and municipal taxrolls and mapped them; her 1997 chapter for the Atlas historique du Québec, mapped with GIS at McGill, sets out to 'saisir … les processus par lesquels la cité se construit'. With Robert Sweeny, Jason Gilliland and others she built MAP (Montréal, l'avenir du passé, begun in 2000), a collective historical GIS in which, as she and François Dufaux wrote in 2014, 'the spatial links place the household on the cadastral lot'. The editors of Historical GIS Research in Canada (2014) name MAP, 'led by' Olson and Sweeny, among the few Canadian HGIS projects since the 1990s, and a Victoria team that includes Gilliland calls her Montreal work 'a model of spatial history'; Sweeny, MAP's co-director, warned in 2009 that 'the ontology of geographic information systems is antithetical to historical understanding'. With Thornton she wrote Peopling the North American City: Montreal, 1840–1900 (2011), which, by its publisher's description, follows families of twelve surnames.
sherry_olson.representative_figures_and_works: Sherry H. Olson; The Depletion Myth: A History of Railroad Use of Timber (1971); “Baltimore Imitates the Spider” (Annals of the AAG, 1979); Baltimore: The Building of an American City (1980; bicentennial edition 1997); with Patricia Thornton and Quoc Thuy Thach, “Dimensions sociales de la mortalité infantile à Montréal au milieu du XIXe siècle” (Annales de démographie historique, 1989); “Occupations and Residential Spaces in Nineteenth-Century Montreal” (Historical Methods, 1989); with David Hanna, “The Social Landscape of Montréal, 1901” (Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 3, plate 30, 1990); “Le peuplement de Montréal” (Atlas historique du Québec: Population et territoire, 1997); with Jason Gilliland, “Claims on Housing Space in Nineteenth-Century Montreal” (Urban History Review, 1998). After 2000: MAP, Montréal, l'avenir du passé (from 2000, with Robert Sweeny and others); “Ethnic Partition of the Work Force in 1840s Montréal” (Labour/Le Travail, 2004); with Gilliland, “Residential Segregation in the Industrializing City” (Urban Geography, 2010); with Gilliland and Danielle Gauvreau, “Did Segregation Increase as the City Expanded?” (Social Science History, 2011); with Patricia Thornton, Peopling the North American City: Montreal, 1840–1900 (2011); with François Dufaux, “Rebuilding a Neighbourhood of Montreal” (2014). Readings: Sweeny (2009); Sager (2012); Horner (2013); Bonnell and Fortin (2014); Lutz, Dunae, Gilliland, Lafreniere and Harvey (2014).
sherry_olson.scope_note: A method entry for historical GIS, not a Quebec-historiography entry: the Quebec self-accounts read for the atlas (Ouellet 1985, Bédard, Bouchard, Rudin, Savard, Linteau) do not name her. Her own words are read in the introduction and acknowledgments of Baltimore (1980), in full in 'Le peuplement de Montréal' (1997), in part in the 2004 Labour/Le Travail research note, and in part in her 2014 chapter with Dufaux; the 1979, 1998, 2010 and 2011 articles are known from their abstracts, and the 1989 Historical Methods article and the 1990 atlas plate at title level only. Peopling the North American City is unread; it is known from publisher copy and the opening paragraphs of Sager's (2012) and Horner's (2013) reviews. In-period reviews of Baltimore exist (AHR, JAH, Technology and Culture, JEH 1981; JIH, Journal of Historical Geography 1982) but were not readable here. The GIS work begins in the 1990s; MAP dates from 2000 and is collective, co-led with Robert Sweeny, whose team built the electronic framework from the Cane map of 1846. She is not presented as the founder of HGIS in Canada: 'pioneering' is the Victoria team's word, and the editors of the 2014 volume list national repositories in the United States and Britain as 'some of the most important work in the field'. The 2014 volume's chapter 2 (Beard, Macfarlane and Clifford) is not used.

bruce_curtis.label: Bruce Curtis
bruce_curtis.date_label: With Corrigan, “Education, Inspection and State Formation” 1985 · Building the Educational State 1988 · True Government by Choice Men? 1992 · The Politics of Population 2001 · “After ‘Canada’” 2009 · Ruling by Schooling Quebec 2012
bruce_curtis.description: A historical sociologist (Carleton University) whose studies of schooling, school inspection and the census in the Canadas read administration as a means of rule. In Building the Educational State (1988), as a reviewer quotes it, education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (p. 110), and the educational state was built 'only through the destruction of a prior educational organization' (p. 15); in True Government by Choice Men? (1992) 'Educational inspection was about state formation: the creation, stabilization and normalisation of relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (p. 32). His census history (2001) holds that 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (p. 305, as Belshaw quotes it), and in a 1996 review he wrote that 'The census simply cannot tell us much about the value of distributed property, about the gendered distribution of property, certainly nothing about inheritance patterns'. Reviewers credited his joining of Foucault's analysis of power to a Marxist theory of state formation but found gender relations missing (Davey 1989; Miller 1993), and Bryan Palmer judged the inspection study, taken as a model, 'overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (1993). In the debate over Ian McKay's liberal order framework, Nancy Christie cites 'Bruce Curtis's important point that what McKay is really describing is governmentality' (2009).
bruce_curtis.representative_figures_and_works: Bruce Curtis (b. 1950); with Philip Corrigan, “Education, Inspection and State Formation: A Preliminary Statement” (CHA Historical Papers, 1985); Building the Educational State: Canada West, 1836–1871 (1988); True Government by Choice Men? Inspection, Education, and State Formation in Canada West (1992); The Politics of Population: State Formation, Statistics, and the Census of Canada, 1840–1875 (2001); “After ‘Canada’: Liberalisms, Social Theory, and Historical Analysis” (2009); Ruling by Schooling Quebec: Conquest to Liberal Governmentality – A Historical Sociology (2012).
bruce_curtis.scope_note: This entry presents Curtis's state-formation studies of schooling, inspection and the census (1985–2001) and their place in the liberal order debate. Read on 2026-10-14: his review of Darroch and Soltow (1996, pp. 107–110) in full, and four in-period or near-period reviews of his books in full: Davey (1989) on Building the Educational State, Miller (1993) and Palmer (1993) on True Government by Choice Men?, and Belshaw (2002) on The Politics of Population; Christie (2009) was re-read for its Curtis passage. His books are unread: his words from them are reviewers' quotations, with the reviewers' page references. The 1985 article with Corrigan, the 2009 chapter and Ruling by Schooling Quebec (2012) are title- or summary-level only. He is a sociologist, not a historian by department; the atlas's moral regulation entry treats his state-formation work as shared ground with the liberal order framework, not membership.

allan_greer.label: Allan Greer
allan_greer.date_label: “Fur-Trade Labour” 1981 · “A Critique of Pentland” and Peasant, Lord, and Merchant 1985 · Colonial Leviathan (ed. with Radforth) 1992 · The Patriots and the People 1993 · Property and Dispossession 2018 · “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” 2019
allan_greer.description: A historian of Lower Canada and colonial North America whose rural social history described a feudal, household-centred habitant society: in 1985 he held that Lower Canadian 'agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production', with part of the surplus 'diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions', a view he set against both Ouellet's routine-bound peasant (1981) and the commercial farmer of Paquet and Wallot, while allowing that 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue' (1985). The same essay, a critique of Clare Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, faulted the staples tradition of Innis and Creighton for confining attention to 'relations of exchange'. With Ian Radforth he edited Colonial Leviathan (1992), on mid-nineteenth-century state formation, which Bryan Palmer found to lack coherence (1993) and which Greer later said 'neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (2019); his history of the 1837 rebellion (1993) is known here through reviewers, who read it as breaking with Ouellet's manipulated peasantry. His later work on 'property formation' (2018) and his 2019 lecture treat settler colonialism as one mode of colonial invasion among several, 'a dominant force in some periods and regions' that 'fades to insignificance in others', while insisting 'I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory'.
allan_greer.representative_figures_and_works: Allan Greer (b. 1950); “Fur-Trade Labour and Lower Canadian Agrarian Structures” (1981); “Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism: A Critique of Pentland” (Labour/Le Travail, 1985); Peasant, Lord, and Merchant: Rural Society in Three Quebec Parishes, 1740–1840 (1985); ed. with Ian Radforth, Colonial Leviathan: State Formation in Mid-Nineteenth-Century Canada (1992); The Patriots and the People: The Rebellion of 1837 in Rural Lower Canada (1993; French translation Habitants et Patriotes, 1997); “Commons and Enclosure in the Colonization of North America” (2012); Property and Dispossession: Natives, Empires and Land in Early Modern North America (2018); “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” (2019).
allan_greer.scope_note: This entry presents Greer's account of rural Lower Canada and the transition to capitalism (1981–85), the state-formation collection (1992) and his later historicising of settler colonialism (2018–19). Read on 2026-10-14: 'Wage Labour and the Transition to Capitalism' (1985, pp. 7–22) and 'Settler Colonialism and Beyond' (2019, pp. 61–86) in full; the introduction to Property and Dispossession (2018, pp. 1–24) on Cambridge Core, which shows no page markers; Palmer's 1993 review of Colonial Leviathan in full. 'Fur-Trade Labour' (1981) was read in full for the Ouellet entry and its critique of Ouellet is carried by edge_989, not repeated here. Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985) and The Patriots and the People (1993) are unread (lending-only copies); the 1985 book is known from its publisher's description and the 1993 book from reviews. Ouellet's review essay on the 1993 book (Histoire sociale / Social History, 1995) is unread, so no reply by Ouellet is quoted. His New France and Jesuit work (The People of New France, 1997; Mohawk Saint, 2005) is not covered.

cole_harris.label: Cole Harris
cole_harris.date_label: The Seigneurial System in Early Canada 1966 · Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1 (editor) 1987 · The Resettlement of British Columbia 1997 · ‘Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia’ 1997–98 · Making Native Space 2002 · ‘Revisiting the Native Land Question’ 2003 · ‘How Did Colonialism Dispossess?’ 2004 · A Bounded Land 2020
cole_harris.description: A Canadian historical geographer of early Canada and of colonialism in British Columbia. He edited the first volume of the Historical Atlas of Canada (1987), whose preface says it sought 'to emphasize the economic and social circumstances of ordinary life rather than the more usual fare of historical atlases' (as quoted by MacDonald, 1990). From the 1990s he wrote British Columbia's colonization as geographical change. Against the 'cultural enrichment hypothesis' of contact-era history he set 'epidemics, increased violence, depopulation, and, for many, a drastic loss of cultural and historical memory' (1997–98). He explained the reserve system as dispossession: its capacity 'rested on raw firepower', its momentum 'came from capital seeking profits and from settlers seeking livelihoods', and its legitimation 'lay with a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery' (2003); in 2004 he argued that the emphasis on culture in studies of colonialism 'tends to obscure other forms of colonial power'. Reviewers found few Native voices in the work: Tina Loo (1998) saw Native peoples 'emerge as victims' in The Resettlement of British Columbia, and Val Napoleon (2004) wrote that Making Native Space 'recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history' and that Harris 'should have incorporated contemporary Aboriginal voices' where history gave way to proposals for the future.
cole_harris.representative_figures_and_works: Cole Harris (R. Cole Harris, 1936–2022); The Seigneurial System in Early Canada (1966); 'Theory and Synthesis in Historical Geography' (Canadian Geographer, 1971); 'The Simplification of Europe Overseas' (Annals of the AAG, 1977); 'The Historical Mind and the Practice of Geography' (1978); ed., with Geoffrey J. Matthews as cartographer and designer, Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1: From the Beginning to 1800 (1987); 'Power, Modernity, and Historical Geography' (Annals of the AAG, 1991); The Resettlement of British Columbia: Essays on Colonialism and Geographical Change (1997; two chapters with Robert Galois and David Demeritt); 'Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia' (BC Studies, 1997/98); Making Native Space: Colonialism, Resistance, and Reserves in British Columbia (2002); 'Revisiting the Native Land Question' (BC Studies forum, 2003, with commentaries by Jo-Anne Fiske and Gordon Gibson and his reply); 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess? Comments from an Edge of Empire' (Annals of the AAG, 2004); A Bounded Land: Reflections on Settler Colonialism in Canada (2020). Readings: MacDonald (1990); Loo (1998); Clayton (2003); Fiske (2003); Napoleon (2004); Perry (2016, later reading).

His own words, read: 'Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia' (BC Studies 115/116, 1997/98, pp. 45–82; pp. 45–47, 56–60, 68–70 and 80–82 read closely, the rest skimmed); 'Revisiting the Native Land Question' with Fiske's and Gibson's commentaries and his reply (BC Studies 138/139, 2003, pp. 137–163, read in full); the abstract of 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess?' Reception read in full: Graham A. MacDonald on the Atlas (Manitoba History 20, 1990, web text); Tina Loo on The Resettlement of British Columbia (BC Studies 117, 1998, pp. 64–67); Daniel Clayton's guest editorial on Making Native Space (BC Studies 138/139, 2003, pp. 5–11); Val Napoleon on Making Native Space (BC Studies 141, 2004, pp. 114–118). Later reading: Perry's 2016 reply in the BC Studies forum on her Colonial Relations (p. 112). Unread: the books themselves (The Seigneurial System, the Atlas, The Resettlement of British Columbia, Making Native Space, A Bounded Land), the 1977 and 1991 Annals essays (known through Clayton's note), the 1994 Ethnohistory article on smallpox, the Canadian Geographer review symposium on Making Native Space (2003; known through Napoleon's summary), and the Native Studies Review forum 'Appraising Cole Harris' Making Native Space' (16:2, 2005; the copy on the University of Saskatchewan site returned 404). He is not presented as a founder of historical geography or of settler-colonial history: the Atlas was a collective work with a cartographer and many contributors, and the texts read do not cite Wolfe. Contested in period by Loo (1998) and Napoleon (2004) on Native voices and agency, by Fiske (2003) on the symbolic, and by the Canadian Geographer symposium (2003, as Napoleon summarises it). adele_perry.label: Adele Perry
adele_perry.date_label: ‘Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men’ 1995 · On the Edge of Empire 2001 · ‘Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History’ 2001 · ‘Women, Racialized People, and the Making of the Liberal Order’ 2009 · Colonial Relations 2015
adele_perry.description: A Canadian historian of gender, race and colonialism in British Columbia and the British Empire. In 1995 she argued that Canadian historians had explained the shortage of white women in the West with a 'scarcity model' and a 'volcano theory' of male sexuality that were 'based on essentialist understandings of both sexuality and race' and belonged to 'colonial discourse itself'. On the Edge of Empire (2001), which she said was 'initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism', studied white miners' homosocial culture, mixed-race relationships and the schemes to bring white women to the colony, and found, in her words as reviewers quote them, 'a sharp disjuncture between colonial discourse and colonial practice on this edge of empire'. Reviewers placed it in whiteness studies and asked for more on Indigenous people: Sarah Carter (2002) wanted the 'social centrality and political agency' of Aboriginal peoples further developed, and Paul Orlowski (2002) found First Nations resistance 'lacking' and a 'binary racial divide' that set aside Chinese workers. In 2016 she described the 2001 book as arguing that British Columbia's history 'is best understood within a comparative framework of settler colonialism'.
adele_perry.representative_figures_and_works: Adele Perry; “‘Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men’: Gender Imbalance, Race, Sexuality, and Sociability in Nineteenth-Century British Columbia” (BC Studies, 1995); “‘Fair Ones of a Purer Caste’: White Women and Colonialism in Nineteenth-Century British Columbia” (1997); “The Historian and the Theorist Revisited” (Histoire sociale/Social History, 2000); On the Edge of Empire: Gender, Race, and the Making of British Columbia, 1849–1871 (2001); “Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History” (BC Studies, 2001/02); “The Autocracy of Love and the Legitimacy of Empire: Intimacy, Power and Scandal in Nineteenth-Century Metlakahtlah” (2004); “Women, Racialized People, and the Making of the Liberal Order in Northern North America” (in Liberalism and Hegemony, 2009); Colonial Relations: The Douglas-Connolly Family and the Nineteenth-Century Imperial World (2015). Readings: Carter (2002); Orlowski (2002); Rutherdale (2002); the BC Studies forum on Colonial Relations (Clayton, Dussart, Devine, Ballantyne, 2016).

philip_huang.label: Philip C. C. Huang
philip_huang.date_label: Modern China founded 1975 · The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China 1985 · The Peasant Family and Rural Development in the Yangzi Delta 1990 · “The Paradigmatic Crisis in Chinese Studies” 1991 · Civil Justice in China 1996 · Code, Custom, and Legal Practice 2001 · exchange with Pomeranz 2002–2003
philip_huang.description: A historian of rural China and Chinese law and the founding editor of Modern China (1975). Huang argued that Ming–Qing commercialization proceeded without capitalist development through involution: output per unit of land rose while the marginal returns to additional labour on family farms diminished, “growth without development”, a claim about marginal rather than average productivity that his critics contested. He took the term from Clifford Geertz’s “agricultural involution” and the mechanism partly from Chayanov, as he acknowledged in 1985 and again in 1991. The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China (1985) and The Peasant Family and Rural Development in the Yangzi Delta (1990) developed the argument, and “The Paradigmatic Crisis in Chinese Studies” (1991) held that Western and Chinese models, Marxist “incipient capitalism” among them, shared assumptions that Chinese evidence made “paradoxical”. His legal histories include Civil Justice in China (1996) and Code, Custom, and Legal Practice in China (2001). He took “practice” from Bourdieu while preferring “the study of practice as historical process” (2005), and rejected culturalist claims, which he attributed to Said, that facts are “no more than representations” (1998). After 2000 he was a prominent critic of Kenneth Pomeranz, arguing that eighteenth-century England and the Yangzi delta stood “at opposite poles in a continuum from development to involution” (2002); Pomeranz answered that involution was “internally inconsistent” (2003).
philip_huang.representative_figures_and_works: Philip C. C. Huang; The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China (1985); The Peasant Family and Rural Development in the Yangzi Delta, 1350–1988 (1990); “The Paradigmatic Crisis in Chinese Studies: Paradoxes in Social and Economic History” (Modern China, 1991); Civil Justice in China (1996); Code, Custom, and Legal Practice in China (2001); “Development or Involution in Eighteenth-Century Britain and China?” (Journal of Asian Studies, 2002) and “Further Thoughts on Eighteenth-Century Britain and China” (2003); “Theory and the Study of Modern Chinese History: Four Traps and a Question” (1998); “Divorce Law Practices and the Origins, Myths, and Realities of Judicial ‘Mediation’ in China” (2005); “Our Sense of Problem” (2016). Founding editor of Modern China (1975). Readings: Mann’s and Duara’s reviews (1986); Pomeranz’s replies (2002, 2003).
philip_huang.scope_note: Involution is presented as Huang defined it in the 1985 book (pp. 7–11 read) and restated it in 1991 (pp. 299–302 and 314–317 read), 2002 (whole article OCRed; selected passages read closely, remaining text searched; map images not inspected) and 2003 (pp. 157–158 and 164–165 read). The 1990 book is unread; it is known through those restatements, Pomeranz’s citation of its pp. 11–17 and Day’s review. Geertz and Chayanov are his acknowledged resources (1985, p. 8; 1991, p. 317) and Boserup a third (1991, n. 9); he redefined Geertz’s term. The exchange with Pomeranz appears once, as two critique arrows. Huang conceded a misplaced decimal in the 1990 book (2003, p. 157) and, as he reports it, Pomeranz’s reply granted declining average returns as cotton displaced grain. Brenner and Isett (2002) and the real-wage study of Allen and colleagues (2011) side partly with him on living standards and divergence, not on the mechanism. His legal histories of 1996 and 2001 are dated only and their arguments are unread here; his use of Bourdieu’s “practice” is taken from a 2005 note and a 1995 article read in part by a second research pass, and his wider later work on practice falls outside this reading. His 1998 critique of Said is read at pp. 193–195. Life dates are not established from texts read.

robert_brenner.label: Robert Brenner
robert_brenner.date_label: “The Civil War Politics of London’s Merchant Community” 1973 · “Agrarian Class Structure and Economic Development in Pre-Industrial Europe” 1976 · “The Origins of Capitalist Development” 1977 · “The Agrarian Roots of European Capitalism” 1982 · The Brenner Debate (Aston and Philpin, eds) 1985 · Merchants and Revolution 1993 · The Economics of Global Turbulence 1998 (book 2006) · with Christopher Isett, “England’s Divergence from China’s Yangzi Delta” 2002
robert_brenner.description: An American historian of early modern Europe whose 'Agrarian Class Structure and Economic Development in Pre-Industrial Europe' (Past and Present, 1976) opened the Brenner debate. Against the 'demographic model' of Postan and Le Roy Ladurie, and the 'commercialization model' it had displaced, he argued that 'it is the structure of class relations, of class power, which will determine the manner and degree to which particular demographic and commercial changes will affect long-run trends in the distribution of income and economic growth — and not vice versa'. Similar population trends accompanied serfdom's decline in the West and its rise in the East. English landlords who consolidated holdings and let them to capitalist tenants made agrarian capitalism; in France secure peasant property and the absolutist state blocked it, so that 'the most complete freedom and property rights for the rural population meant poverty'. A companion essay in New Left Review (1977) charged Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein with a 'neo-Smithian' Marxism that made trade, not class relations, the motor of development, and acknowledged his 'great debt' to Dobb's critique of Sweezy. Postan and Hatcher (1978) replied that he misrepresented historians who had never given population 'an all-determining role'; Le Roy Ladurie found him 'extremely insular'; Croot and Parker doubted his England–France contrast; the Marxist Guy Bois welcomed the attack on 'the Malthusian model' but called the approach 'political Marxism', 'a voluntarist vision of history' (as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos, 1990). Brenner's reply (1982) restated the argument as one about 'social-property systems'. Introducing the collected debate (1985), Hilton read it as a continuation of the Dobb–Sweezy transition debate. Merchants and Revolution (1993) gave the English Revolution what Gentles called 'a new social interpretation', centred on London's colonial merchants; later work turned to the postwar world economy (1998) and, with Christopher Isett (2002), answered Pomeranz on England and the Yangzi delta.
robert_brenner.representative_figures_and_works: Robert Brenner (b. 1943); 'The Civil War Politics of London's Merchant Community' (Past and Present 58, 1973); 'Agrarian Class Structure and Economic Development in Pre-Industrial Europe' (Past and Present 70, 1976); 'The Origins of Capitalist Development: A Critique of Neo-Smithian Marxism' (New Left Review I/104, 1977); 'The Agrarian Roots of European Capitalism' (Past and Present 97, 1982); T. H. Aston and C. H. E. Philpin (eds), The Brenner Debate (1985), with R. H. Hilton's introduction; Merchants and Revolution: Commercial Change, Political Conflict, and London's Overseas Traders, 1550–1653 (1993); The Economics of Global Turbulence (New Left Review I/229, 1998; book 2006); with Christopher Isett, 'England's Divergence from China's Yangzi Delta' (Journal of Asian Studies, 2002). Respondents and readers: M. M. Postan and John Hatcher (1978); Patricia Croot and David Parker (1978); Heide Wunder (1978); Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie (1978); Guy Bois (1978); J. P. Cooper (1978); Arnošt Klíma (1979); Chris Harman (1989; debate with Brenner, 2004); Ian Gentles and Alex Callinicos (1994); Ellen Meiksins Wood (1996); Kenneth Pomeranz (2000); Prasannan Parthasarathi (2011); Thomas Leng (2024).
robert_brenner.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-18: 'Agrarian Class Structure' (1976): the whole article (pp. 30–75, page numbers from the running heads) OCRed; pp. 30–34, 42–43, 47, 53, 56, 61–62 and 71–75 read closely, the remaining pages searched by keyword and skimmed; wording cross-checked against a transcription; 'The Origins of Capitalist Development' (1977) in full, in a transcription without New Left Review pages, cited by section; the 1985 volume's responses and Brenner's 1982 reply only in Cambridge Core's open chapter openings, with Bois's coinage of 'political Marxism' as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990). The journal texts of 1978–82 are unread. Readers: Harman (1989, in part); the Harman–Brenner exchange of November 2004 (in full; Brenner's contributions were reworked for print); the openings of Gentles's and Callinicos's 1994 reviews; Wood's 1996 abstract; Leng (2024); Parthasarathi (2011, pp. 3–5) and Allen (2009, p. 4) in their publishers' excerpts. Merchants and Revolution, The Economics of Global Turbulence and the 1973 article are unread; their content is given only through named readers. The 2002 article with Isett was read in its opening and, for revision 1.144, in a truncated repost. He is not presented as the first to give class structure priority: he wrote that the view 'obviously derives from Marx's arguments', acknowledged Dobb, and used Tawney's and Hilton's evidence; Postan and Hatcher wrote that his 'essentials … have been put forward many times before'. The label 'political Marxism' was Bois's criticism in 1978 before it named a school. The debate as a whole is held by the group entry capitalismdebates; the respondents' critiques are drawn from it to this entry. The Pomeranz exchange (2000–2002) is later and smaller. Not to be confused with namesakes on Wikidata (an Austrian physicist, a German mining engineer).

joel_mokyr.label: Joel Mokyr
joel_mokyr.date_label: “Demand vs. Supply in the Industrial Revolution” 1977 · The Lever of Riches 1990 · editor’s introduction, The British Industrial Revolution 1999 · The Gifts of Athena 2002 · Max Weber Lecture on the European Enlightenment 2007 · The Enlightened Economy 2009 · with Kelly and Ó Gráda, “Precocious Albion” 2014 · A Culture of Growth 2016 · “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” 2023 · with Tabellini, “Why China and Europe Diverged” 2023 · economics prize 2025
joel_mokyr.description: An economic historian of technology at Northwestern University who explained sustained growth by the growth of “useful knowledge”. In 1977 he judged demand factors “of a secondary order of importance” in the Industrial Revolution. His 1999 introduction defended the term against the charge that it was “a concept too many” and defined the Industrial Revolution as “a clustering of macroinventions leading to an acceleration in microinventions”. Two drafts of 2002, which say they adapt The Gifts of Athena (2002; unread here, though its reviewer Zorina Khan reports the same scheme), divided useful knowledge into “propositional” knowledge of natural regularities and “prescriptive” instructions (February), and called the Enlightenment’s contribution “the Industrial Enlightenment”, “the key to sustained and accelerating invention”, finding Pomeranz’s coal and New World land “not incorrect but by itself” unable to explain the gap (October). In a 2007 lecture the Enlightenment kept the early Industrial Revolution from “fizzling out”. Reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), C. Knick Harley wondered whether “causation from Enlightenment … to economic change actually existed”, while finding that the book made “a strong case” that “the history of ideas and their place in society needs to be at the core of the story” (2010). In Claude Diebolt’s account of A Culture of Growth (2016), culture works “as the invisible hand”, in a phenomenon “related to an elite” of philosophers, scientists, engineers, instrument makers and industrialists; Diebolt regretted “the lack of in-depth consideration of the German language literature” (2017). With Morgan Kelly and Cormac Ó Gráda he answered Robert Allen’s high-wage explanation with British workers’ human capital (2014), and found that across England’s 41 counties industrialisation occurred where wages began low and mechanical skills high (2023). With Guido Tabellini he traced China’s and Europe’s political divergence to clans and corporations (2023). In 2025 he was awarded a share of the economics prize in memory of Alfred Nobel, cited “for having identified the prerequisites for sustained growth through technological progress”.

e_a_wrigley.label: E. A. Wrigley
e_a_wrigley.date_label: Cambridge Group founded (with Laslett) 1964 · with Schofield, The Population History of England 1981 · Ellen McArthur lectures 1987 · Continuity, Chance and Change 1988 · with Davies, Oeppen and Schofield, English Population History from Family Reconstitution 1997 · Poverty, Progress, and Population 2004 · Energy and the English Industrial Revolution 2010 · The Path to Sustained Growth 2016
e_a_wrigley.description: A historical demographer and economic historian at Cambridge, who founded the Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure with Peter Laslett in 1964. With Roger Schofield he reconstructed England’s population from the registers of 404 parishes by “back projection”, making it “possible for the first time” to follow “a secular cycle of population development” and its relation to economic change (1981); a family-reconstitution study, a technique perfected by Louis Henry, was its complement (1997). He called the industrial revolution his “first main research interest”, to which he “returned increasingly” after years of population history. In Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), from his 1987 Ellen McArthur lectures, he questioned it as “a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon”: growth came from two sets of forces with “only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time”, as an “organic economy” bounded by the productivity of the land met a new one using mineral energy. Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010) asked “not how the period of more rapid growth began, but why it did not come to an end”, without offering energy as the only explanation: there could be “no single, ‘true’ account”, and to downplay institutional and scientific explanations would be “presumptuous and mildly ridiculous”. Mining coal “provided the solution” (2016). He judged Rostow’s “take-off” “now almost impossible to maintain” (2004). Berg and Hudson questioned causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s aggregate studies (1990). Readers set his energy argument beside Pomeranz’s coal (Mokyr in a draft of 2002, Huang in 2002, Clark and Jacks in 2007), and Wong said that China Transformed had followed his arguments on coal (2016).

Schofield, The Population History of England, 1541–1871: A Reconstruction (1981); People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change: The Character of the Industrial Revolution in England (1988); with R. S. Davies, J. E. Oeppen and R. S. Schofield, English Population History from Family Reconstitution, 1580–1837 (1997); Poverty, Progress, and Population (2004); Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010); “Energy and the English Industrial Revolution” (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 2013); The Path to Sustained Growth (2016). Co-founder, with Peter Laslett, of the Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure (1964). Readers and critics: Maxine Berg and Pat Hudson (1990); Joel Mokyr and Philip Huang (2002); Gregory Clark and David Jacks (2007); R. Bin Wong (2016).

Wong’s statement that China Transformed followed Wrigley is his 2016 retrospective. The wider argument about why industrialisation happened in Britain is held by the debate entry capitalismdebates; his population work stays on demography/aggregate_population.

jan_de_vries.label: Jan de Vries
jan_de_vries.date_label: The Economy of Europe in an Age of Crisis, 1600–1750 1976 · “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” 1994 · with van der Woude, The First Modern Economy 1997 · The Industrious Revolution 2008
jan_de_vries.description: An economic historian of the Netherlands and early modern Europe at Berkeley. The Economy of Europe in an Age of Crisis (1976) studied “the last great epoch before the onset of industrialization”; Pomeranz later called it “a good general critique of the overseas extraction thesis”. His “industrious revolution”, proposed in his Economic History Association presidential address published in 1994, was meant “to place the Industrial Revolution in a broader historical setting”: “a household-level change with important demand-side features that preceded the Industrial Revolution, a supply-side phenomenon”. In The Industrious Revolution (2008) he dated it to “roughly 1650–1850”, when households in north-western Europe and British North America reallocated “the time of their members” to earn money and to buy goods. He took the term from Akira Hayami, who had contrasted Japan’s labour-intensive path with Western industrialisation. He built the argument on the revisionist macroeconomics that cut British growth estimates “by more than half”, on the Cambridge Group’s finding that the western European nuclear family long predated industrialisation, and on Becker’s household economics; against a supply-side orthodoxy he illustrated with Mokyr, he sought to “restore demand as one of the cutting blades of Marshall’s supply and demand scissors” (2008). With Ad van der Woude he presented the Dutch Republic as “the first modern economy” (1997), against historians who saw its achievement as “backward looking”; van Zanden doubted that Dutch growth was much faster than England’s (2002). Pomeranz used the industrious revolution for Chinese households (2000). Reviewers found The Industrious Revolution “on all the main points, convincing” (Voth, 2009), or thought it made consumption a new “deus ex machina” and played down power between the sexes (van Nederveen Meerkerk, 2009). From the history of papermaking, Leonard Rosenband challenged its chronology and mechanism: paperworkers already laboured long hours at the outset of the period, and women and adolescents worked for wages in paper mills long before it (2016).

Readers and critics: Kenneth Pomeranz (2000); Philip Huang (2002); Jan Luiten van Zanden (2002); Hans-Joachim Voth and Elise van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009); Leonard Rosenband (2016).

r_bin_wong.label: R. Bin Wong
r_bin_wong.date_label: with Will, Nourish the People 1991 · China Transformed 1997 · with Rosenthal, Before and Beyond Divergence 2011 · “Divergence Displaced” 2016
r_bin_wong.description: A historian of China at UCLA whose China Transformed (1997) compared Chinese and European economic change, state formation and popular protest without treating Europe as the norm. As Joel Mokyr read it, Wong held that before 1800 Europe and China shared “Smithian expansion, rural industry, population expansion, a growth in consumer demand”, and that the “supply-driven Industrial Revolution that followed the demand-led Industrious Revolution in Europe did not happen in China” (1997, p. 31, as Mokyr quotes it). Kenneth Pomeranz wrote that he was “following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed”, while giving “greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures” (2000). Wong later said that the book had located Europe’s difference in science and technology, “following arguments of E. A. Wrigley” on coal (2016). With Jean-Laurent Rosenthal, in Before and Beyond Divergence (2011), he turned to “political fragmentation in Europe and the presence of an unitary state for the Chinese empire”: war drew European craft production into cities, so that the question became “why was industrialization more likely to occur in Western Europe than in China” (his 2016 account); as Debin Ma reported the mechanism, higher urban wages there biased innovation towards saving labour. Ma judged the book “a good contribution in the Great Divergence debate” but found this “stimulating and striking hypothesis” “supported by fairly meager evidence in the chapter” (2012). In “Divergence Displaced” (2016) he judged Brenner’s agrarian social relations, Pomeranz’s coal and colonies and his own earlier book alike open to “non-falsifiability”. Mokyr had objected that “Bin Wong does not cite any book by Needham” (2002 draft).
